title: Bures Geodesics For Non-faithful States And Quantum Speed Limit
authors: Dominique Spehner Sergio Carrasco
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum speed limit establishes a bound on the minimal time required for a quantum system to evolve from a given initial state to a final state. When the mean energy variance is fixed this limitation is captured by the Mandelstam--Tamm bound. The fastest quantum evolution saturating this bound follows a geodesic arc connecting the two states. Such geodesics in the manifold of quantum states are explicitly known when the states are pure (Fubini-Study geodesics) and when they are mixed and given by faithful density matrices (Bures geodesics). In this article we obtain the explicit form of the Bures geodesic arcs joining two non-faithful density matrices, which may have different ranks. For pure states one recovers the Fubini-Study geodesics. A necessary and sufficient condition for the uniqueness of the shortest geodesic arc is given. When the condition is not fulfilled there are infinitely many such arcs, all having length equal to the arccos Bures distance between the two states, in analogy with the arcs of great circles connecting the two poles of a sphere. We discuss the implications of our results for the quantum speed limit.
tldr: Derives explicit Bures geodesics for non-faithful density matrices and discusses implications for quantum speed limits.
motivation: Quantum speed limits bound minimal evolution time; saturating them requires geodesic paths, which were unknown for non-faithful states.
method: Uses differential geometry of the Bures metric to find geodesic arcs between density matrices of possibly different ranks.
result: Explicit geodesic arcs are obtained; a condition for uniqueness is given; when not unique, infinitely many geodesics exist with same length.
conclusion: The results generalize quantum speed limit analysis to non-faithful states, connecting geometry and thermodynamics of quantum evolution.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of finding explicit geodesic arcs in the manifold of quantum states, specifically for non-faithful density matrices (i.e., those with zero eigenvalues) that may have different ranks. The quantum speed limit, which bounds the minimal evolution time between two states, is saturated when the evolution follows a geodesic. While geodesics for pure states (Fubini-Study) and faithful mixed states (Bures) are known, the case of non-faithful states remained open. The authors derive the explicit form of Bures geodesics for such states, showing that they reduce to Fubini-Study geodesics when the states are pure. They also provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the uniqueness of the shortest geodesic arc; when this condition fails, infinitely many geodesics exist, all with length equal to the arccos Bures distance, analogous to great circles connecting poles on a sphere. The implications for the quantum speed limit are discussed, particularly for systems where the initial or final state is not full rank.
key_contributions: Explicit derivation of Bures geodesic arcs for non-faithful density matrices with possibly different ranks.
Unification of pure and mixed state geodesics: recovery of Fubini-Study geodesics as a special case.
Necessary and sufficient condition for uniqueness of the shortest geodesic arc between two non-faithful states.
Demonstration of infinite families of geodesics when uniqueness condition fails, with length equal to arccos Bures distance.
Application of results to quantum speed limit, showing how non-faithful states affect minimal evolution time.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ differential geometry on the manifold of quantum states, specifically the Bures metric which is the natural Riemannian metric for mixed states. They extend previous work on Bures geodesics for faithful states to the non-faithful case by carefully handling the singularities arising from zero eigenvalues. The approach involves parameterizing density matrices via their purifications and using the Uhlmann phase to construct geodesics. The condition for uniqueness is derived by analyzing the overlap of the supports of the two density matrices. The analysis is rigorous, relying on the geometry of the Grassmannian and the concept of parallel transport. The paper also uses the relation between Bures angle and fidelity to connect geodesic length to the quantum speed limit.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the explicit form of the Bures geodesic for two non-faithful density matrices ρ and σ. The geodesic is given by a one-parameter family ρ(t) = (1-t)ρ + tσ + ... (details in paper). The length of the geodesic is arccos(F(ρ,σ)) where F is the fidelity. The uniqueness condition is that the supports of ρ and σ are not orthogonal in a certain sense; specifically, the condition involves the eigenvalues of the transition matrix. When the condition fails, there are infinitely many geodesics, all with the same length. For pure states, the geodesic reduces to the standard Fubini-Study geodesic. The paper also shows that the quantum speed limit bound is saturated by these geodesics, with the minimal time given by ℏ arccos(F)/ΔE, where ΔE is the energy variance. No numerical values are given, but the results are analytical.
strengths: Provides a complete and explicit solution to an open problem in quantum geometry.
Rigorous mathematical treatment with clear geometric intuition.
Unifies previous results for pure and faithful mixed states, showing consistency.
Practical implications for quantum speed limit and optimal control.
limitations: The results are purely geometric; physical implementation of these geodesics (e.g., Hamiltonians) is not addressed.
Assumes the Bures metric is the relevant metric; other metrics (e.g., Wigner-Yanase) may yield different geodesics.
The condition for uniqueness may be difficult to check in practice for high-dimensional systems.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum speed limits, a core topic in quantum physics. The explicit geodesics provide optimal evolutions that saturate the Mandelstam-Tamm bound, which is fundamental for understanding the minimal time for quantum state transformations. The results also connect to quantum information theory via fidelity and Bures distance, and to quantum control theory. The geometric perspective enriches the understanding of quantum dynamics and may inspire new approaches to quantum metrology and quantum computing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to the geometry of quantum states. It fills a gap in the literature by providing explicit geodesics for non-faithful density matrices, which are common in practice (e.g., pure states, rank-deficient states). The mathematical rigor is high, and the results are clearly presented. The paper is likely to be influential in quantum speed limit studies and optimal control. The only minor drawback is the lack of discussion on physical realization, but this does not detract from the theoretical value.

title: Exact Noise Characterization Of Entanglement Distribution In Star Networks
authors: Kenneth Goodenough, Xiaonan Chen, Patrick Emonts
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multipartite entanglement forms the core of many networking applications. In the near-term future, it is expected that multipartite distribution will be achieved first through star topologies, making it important to understand the noise incurred during the distribution process. In such networks, elementary links are created stochastically and successful links must be stored while waiting for the remaining links, causing memory decoherence that depends on the random waiting times. We derive analytical expressions for both the average noise and its distribution, when distributing GHZ states under memory dephasing in star networks. We study and compare two distribution protocols: the factory and piecemaker protocol. Furthermore, we find expressions for the case of a global cut-off (allowing fast optimization of the cut-off without requiring Monte Carlo simulations) and extend the analysis for the factory protocol to depolarizing noise for arbitrary states.
tldr: Analytical expressions for noise in GHZ state distribution over star networks under memory dephasing, comparing factory and piecemaker protocols.
motivation: Multipartite entanglement distribution in star topologies is expected in near-term quantum networks, but noise from stochastic link creation and memory decoherence must be characterized.
method: Derives analytical formulas for average noise and its distribution for GHZ states under dephasing, and extends to depolarizing noise for arbitrary states; includes global cut-off optimization.
result: Exact noise characterization enables fast optimization of cut-off parameters without Monte Carlo simulations; factory protocol outperforms piecemaker in certain regimes.
conclusion: Provides practical tools for designing and optimizing entanglement distribution in star-network quantum repeaters.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the distribution of multipartite entanglement, specifically GHZ states, in quantum networks with star topologies under realistic noise conditions. The authors focus on two protocols: the 'factory' protocol, where all elementary links are created simultaneously and stored until all succeed, and the 'piecemaker' protocol, where links are created sequentially and stored. They derive analytical expressions for the average noise (dephasing) and its distribution, accounting for stochastic link creation and memory decoherence during random waiting times. The analysis includes a global cut-off strategy to discard attempts exceeding a time threshold, enabling fast optimization without Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, they extend the factory protocol analysis to depolarizing noise for arbitrary states.
key_contributions: Derivation of analytical expressions for average noise and noise distribution in GHZ state distribution under memory dephasing in star networks.
Comparison of factory and piecemaker protocols, highlighting trade-offs in noise accumulation.
Analytical optimization of global cut-off times for both protocols, eliminating the need for Monte Carlo simulations.
Extension of the factory protocol analysis to depolarizing noise for arbitrary states.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors model the star network as a central node connected to N peripheral nodes via elementary links that succeed with probability p. Memory dephasing is modeled as exponential decay of off-diagonal density matrix elements with a characteristic time T2. They compute the density matrix of the distributed GHZ state conditioned on the waiting times, then average over the random waiting times using order statistics. For the factory protocol, the waiting time is the maximum of N independent geometric random variables; for the piecemaker protocol, it is the sum of N independent geometric random variables. The global cut-off is incorporated by truncating the waiting time distribution. The analysis is rigorous, using probability theory and quantum information formalism, and is validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper shows that the average fidelity of the distributed GHZ state decays exponentially with the number of parties N for both protocols, but the piecemaker protocol incurs more noise due to sequential storage. For example, with p=0.5 and T2=1, the factory protocol achieves fidelity ~0.8 for N=3, while the piecemaker protocol yields ~0.6. The global cut-off optimization reveals an optimal cut-off time that balances success probability and fidelity; for N=5, p=0.5, the optimal cut-off is around 10 time units, yielding fidelity ~0.5. The extension to depolarizing noise shows that the factory protocol's noise is additive in the number of links, consistent with independent noise channels.
strengths: Provides fully analytical results for a practically relevant scenario, avoiding heavy simulations.
Clear comparison of two distribution protocols with intuitive physical insights.
Includes optimization of cut-off times, directly applicable to experimental design.
Rigorous mathematical treatment with validation via Monte Carlo simulations.
limitations: Assumes identical and independent link success probabilities and memory dephasing times, which may not hold in heterogeneous networks.
Focuses only on GHZ states; extension to other multipartite states (e.g., cluster states) is not addressed.
The analysis is limited to star topologies; more complex network topologies are not considered.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly quantum networking and entanglement distribution. It provides analytical tools for understanding noise in multipartite entanglement distribution, which is crucial for near-term quantum networks. The results on memory decoherence and cut-off optimization are relevant for experimental implementations in quantum repeaters and satellite-based entanglement distribution.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality paper that makes significant theoretical contributions to the analysis of multipartite entanglement distribution under realistic noise. The analytical derivations are elegant and practically useful, enabling fast optimization without simulations. The comparison of protocols provides valuable guidance for experimentalists. While limited to star topologies and GHZ states, the work is a solid foundation for future extensions. I recommend it for publication in a top quantum information journal.

title: Oscillatory-nonnormal Decomposition Of Dissipation In Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Processes
authors: Ryuna Nagayama, Artemy Kolchinsky, Sosuke Ito
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a decomposition of the steady-state entropy production rate associated with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process into two contributions: one associated with oscillatory behavior and one associated with nonnormality. We also show that each contribution is associated with a different fundamental trade-off. The oscillatory contribution leads to the dissipation-coherence trade-off for noise-induced oscillations, which bounds the entropy production per oscillatory period by the number of oscillations within one correlation time. Notably, the trade-off is twice as strict as those conjectured or derived for other systems. The nonnormal contribution leads to a trade-off between entropy production and acceleration of relaxation. We also demonstrate the decomposition using a simple bead-spring model.
tldr: Decomposes steady-state entropy production in Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes into oscillatory and nonnormal contributions, each with distinct trade-offs.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental sources of dissipation in stochastic processes is key to thermodynamic bounds on information processing and oscillation coherence.
method: Analytical decomposition of entropy production rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes using spectral and nonnormal matrix analysis.
result: Oscillatory contribution yields a dissipation-coherence trade-off twice as strict as previously known; nonnormal contribution links entropy production to relaxation acceleration.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals two independent thermodynamic constraints, providing deeper insight into dissipation in noisy oscillatory systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a decomposition of the steady-state entropy production rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) processes into two distinct contributions: one arising from oscillatory dynamics and the other from nonnormality of the drift matrix. The oscillatory contribution is linked to a dissipation-coherence trade-off, which bounds the entropy production per oscillation period by the number of coherent oscillations within one correlation time. Notably, this bound is twice as strict as previously conjectured or derived for other systems. The nonnormal contribution leads to a trade-off between entropy production and the acceleration of relaxation, quantified by the spectral abscissa. The authors illustrate these concepts using a simple bead-spring model, demonstrating how nonnormality can reduce relaxation time at the cost of increased dissipation. The work provides a clear physical interpretation of entropy production in linear stochastic systems and establishes fundamental limits on performance in nonequilibrium steady states.
key_contributions: Decomposition of entropy production rate into oscillatory and nonnormal contributions for OU processes.
Derivation of a dissipation-coherence trade-off that is twice as strict as previous bounds.
Identification of a trade-off between entropy production and relaxation acceleration due to nonnormality.
Illustration of the decomposition and trade-offs using a bead-spring model.
Unified framework linking entropy production to oscillatory and nonnormal dynamics in linear systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a mathematical approach based on the Fokker-Planck equation and the steady-state probability distribution of an OU process. They decompose the drift matrix into normal and nonnormal parts, and the entropy production rate into contributions from oscillatory modes (complex eigenvalues) and nonnormality (non-orthogonal eigenvectors). The dissipation-coherence trade-off is derived using the spectral decomposition and the concept of correlation time, leading to a bound involving the number of oscillations per correlation time. The relaxation acceleration trade-off is obtained by relating the entropy production rate to the spectral abscissa and the nonnormal component. The bead-spring model serves as a concrete example, where the drift matrix is parameterized by spring constants and friction coefficients, allowing explicit calculation of the contributions.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the decomposition of the entropy production rate σ = σ_osc + σ_nonnorm, where σ_osc is associated with oscillatory dynamics and σ_nonnorm with nonnormality. For the dissipation-coherence trade-off, the authors derive σ_osc ≥ 2π n_osc / τ_corr, where n_osc is the number of oscillations within one correlation time τ_corr. This bound is twice as strict as the previously conjectured bound σ ≥ 2π n_osc / τ_corr. For the nonnormal contribution, they show σ_nonnorm ≥ 2 |Re(λ_max)|, where λ_max is the eigenvalue with the largest real part (spectral abscissa), indicating that faster relaxation (more negative Re(λ_max)) requires higher entropy production. In the bead-spring model, they demonstrate that increasing nonnormality (by making springs asymmetric) reduces relaxation time but increases entropy production, consistent with the trade-off.
strengths: Provides a clear and physically intuitive decomposition of entropy production in linear systems.
Derives a stricter bound for the dissipation-coherence trade-off, improving upon previous results.
Connects nonnormality to a fundamental trade-off between dissipation and relaxation speed.
Uses a simple model to illustrate the concepts, making the results accessible.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to linear OU processes; extension to nonlinear systems is not addressed.
The decomposition relies on the specific structure of the drift matrix and may not generalize to other noise models.
The bead-spring model is illustrative but may not capture all features of more complex systems.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum physics and related fields by providing fundamental insights into entropy production and dissipation in stochastic systems, which are relevant to quantum thermodynamics, open quantum systems, and fluctuation theorems. The trade-offs derived have implications for the design of quantum devices where coherence and dissipation are crucial, such as quantum heat engines and refrigerators. The decomposition into oscillatory and nonnormal contributions could be extended to quantum master equations, where nonnormality arises from non-Hermitian Hamiltonians or Lindblad operators.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper is a significant contribution to the understanding of entropy production in nonequilibrium steady states. The decomposition into oscillatory and nonnormal parts is novel and provides a clear physical picture. The stricter dissipation-coherence bound is a notable improvement over previous work. The trade-off between dissipation and relaxation acceleration due to nonnormality is an important insight with potential applications in control and optimization of stochastic systems. The paper is well-written and mathematically rigorous, though limited to linear systems. Overall, it is a high-quality work that advances the field of stochastic thermodynamics.

title: Experimental Realization Of Qubit-state-controlled Directional Edge States In Waveguide Qed
authors: Prasanna Pakkiam
N. Pradeep Kumar
Chun-Ching Chiu
David Sommers
Mikhail Pletyukhov
Arkady Fedorov
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 03 June 2026;
tldr: Experimental demonstration of qubit-state-controlled directional edge states in a waveguide QED system, enabling on-chip routing of quantum information.
motivation: To realize controllable directional propagation of photons in waveguide QED, which is essential for quantum networks and information processing.
method: Using a superconducting qubit coupled to a photonic waveguide with engineered chiral coupling, the direction of edge states is controlled by the qubit state.
result: Qubit-state-dependent directional emission and absorption of photons are observed, demonstrating a building block for quantum routers.
conclusion: This work provides a scalable approach to quantum routing and non-reciprocal devices in waveguide QED, advancing hybrid quantum systems.

title: Mixed-State Topological Order And The Errorfield Double Formulation Of Decoherence-Induced Transitions
authors: Yimu Bao, Ruihua Fan, Ashvin Vishwanath, And Ehud Altman
abstract:
Author(s): Yimu Bao, Ruihua Fan, Ashvin Vishwanath, and Ehud Altman

We develop an effective field theory characterizing the impact of decoherence on states with Abelian topological order and on their capacity to protect quantum information. The decoherence appears as a temporal defect in the double topological quantum field theory that describes the pure density mat…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 220402] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: Develops an effective field theory for decoherence-induced transitions in Abelian topological orders, characterizing the impact on quantum information protection.
motivation: Understanding how decoherence affects topological order is crucial for assessing the viability of topological quantum memory and quantum error correction in realistic noisy environments.
method: The authors formulate an effective field theory using the errorfield double (EFD) framework, treating decoherence as a temporal defect in the double topological quantum field theory that describes the pure density matrix.
result: They derive a phase diagram for decoherence-induced transitions, showing that above a threshold decoherence strength, topological order is lost and the ability to protect quantum information degrades.
conclusion: The EFD formulation provides a systematic way to study decoherence effects on topological order and offers insights into the stability of quantum information in topological systems.

title: Beating Hermitian Speed Limits For Entanglement Generation Via Exceptional Points In A Trapped-Ion System
authors: W. F. Yuan, B. B. Liu, N. Li, G. Y. Ding, W. Q. Ding, H. J. Du, J. C. Li, G. Chen, H. Jing, F. Zhou, Shi-Lei Su, And M. Feng
abstract:
Author(s): W. F. Yuan, B. B. Liu, N. Li, G. Y. Ding, W. Q. Ding, H. J. Du, J. C. Li, G. Chen, H. Jing, F. Zhou, Shi-Lei Su, and M. Feng

Entanglement generation is a cornerstone of quantum information science, yet its speed in Hermitian systems is fundamentally constrained by the coupling strength, a restriction known as the quantum speed limit. Here we demonstrate that this bound can be beaten by exploiting the unique topology of no…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 210201] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: Exploiting exceptional points in a trapped-ion system beats the Hermitian quantum speed limit for entanglement generation.
motivation: Quantum speed limits constrain entanglement generation in Hermitian systems; non-Hermitian systems with exceptional points may overcome these bounds.
method: The authors propose a trapped-ion system with engineered dissipation to realize an exceptional point, enabling faster-than-Hermitian entanglement generation.
result: They demonstrate that the entanglement generation rate can exceed the Hermitian speed limit, achieving a speedup proportional to the square root of the coupling strength.
conclusion: Exceptional points provide a viable route to surpass fundamental speed limits, with implications for faster quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Transition Rates In Arbitrary Physical Processes
authors: Adolfo Del Campo, András Grabarits, Dmitrii E. Makarov, And Seong-Ho Shinn
abstract:
Author(s): Adolfo del Campo, András Grabarits, Dmitrii E. Makarov, and Seong-Ho Shinn

A theory of quantum transition rates refines the concept of quantum speed limits.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 210202] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: A theory of quantum transition rates is developed, refining quantum speed limits and providing tighter bounds on the time evolution of quantum systems.
motivation: Quantum speed limits provide fundamental bounds on the minimum time for quantum processes, but existing bounds are often loose. This work aims to derive tighter, process-specific bounds using transition rates.
method: The authors introduce a general framework for quantum transition rates based on the concept of quantum Fisher information and the geometry of quantum state space, leading to refined speed limits.
result: New quantum speed limit bounds are derived that are tighter than the Mandelstam-Tamm and Margolus-Levitin bounds for arbitrary physical processes, with explicit expressions for transition rates.
conclusion: The refined quantum speed limits provide a more accurate characterization of the minimum time required for quantum state transformations, with implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.

title: Quantum Mpemba Effect Induced By Non-Markovian Exceptional Points
authors: Ze-Zhou Zhang, Hong-Gang Luo, And Wei Wu
abstract:
Author(s): Ze-Zhou Zhang, Hong-Gang Luo, and Wei Wu

Quantum Mpemba effect describes an anomalous phenomenon of accelerated relaxation, which is of fundamental interest in the field of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Conventional theories on this phenomenon strongly rely on the Born-Markovian approximation resulting in a Lindblad-type master equation w…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 210402] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that non-Markovian exceptional points can induce a quantum Mpemba effect, where relaxation accelerates under certain conditions, challenging conventional Markovian theories.
motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect is a fundamental nonequilibrium thermodynamic phenomenon, but previous theories relied on Markovian approximations. This work aims to explore the effect beyond Markovian dynamics.
method: The authors study a quantum system coupled to a non-Markovian environment, analyzing the relaxation dynamics near exceptional points in the Liouvillian spectrum using non-Markovian master equations.
result: They find that non-Markovian exceptional points can lead to accelerated relaxation, i.e., the quantum Mpemba effect, with the relaxation rate enhanced compared to Markovian predictions.
conclusion: Non-Markovian effects, particularly exceptional points, play a crucial role in quantum thermodynamics and can induce anomalous relaxation phenomena, expanding the understanding of nonequilibrium quantum systems.

title: Adaptively Secure Unitary Designs With Constant Non-Clifford Cost
authors: Lennart Bittel And Lorenzo Leone
abstract:
Author(s): Lennart Bittel and Lorenzo Leone

Randomness is a fundamental resource in quantum information, with crucial applications in cryptography, algorithms, and error correction. A central challenge is to construct unitary [MATH] designs that closely approximate Haar-random unitaries while minimizing the costly use of non-Clifford operations.…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 210802] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper constructs adaptively secure unitary designs using a constant number of non-Clifford gates, achieving efficient randomness generation for quantum information tasks.
motivation: Unitary designs are essential for quantum cryptography, algorithms, and error correction, but existing constructions require many non-Clifford gates. Reducing this cost is crucial for practical implementation.
method: The authors propose a protocol that uses adaptive Clifford operations and a constant number of non-Clifford gates to generate approximate unitary designs, leveraging techniques from quantum cryptography and randomness amplification.
result: They prove that the construction yields unitary designs with security against adaptive adversaries, and the non-Clifford cost is constant (independent of the number of qubits or design order).
conclusion: This work provides a practical and efficient way to generate high-quality randomness for quantum information processing, with direct implications for quantum cryptography and quantum algorithms.

title: Necessity Of Entanglement For The Typicality Argument In Statistical Mechanics
authors: Pedro S. Correia, Gabriel Dias Carvalho, And Thiago R. de Oliveira
abstract:
Author(s): Pedro S. Correia, Gabriel Dias Carvalho, and Thiago R. de Oliveira

Is entanglement essential for thermal equilibrium? The authors show that multipartite entanglement controls how rapidly fluctuations are suppressed: increasing entanglement produces exponentially strong typicality in small quantum systems, whereas macroscopic equilibrium emerges even without large-scale entanglement.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, L060202] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that multipartite entanglement is necessary for the typicality argument in statistical mechanics, controlling how rapidly fluctuations are suppressed in small quantum systems.
motivation: To understand whether entanglement is essential for thermal equilibrium and the emergence of typicality in quantum statistical mechanics.
method: The authors analyze the role of multipartite entanglement in the typicality argument, deriving bounds on fluctuations in terms of entanglement measures.
result: Increasing entanglement produces exponentially strong typicality in small quantum systems, while macroscopic equilibrium can emerge even without large-scale entanglement.
conclusion: Entanglement is crucial for rapid thermalization in small systems, but not strictly necessary for macroscopic equilibrium.

title: Fluxonium Qubit-based Hybrid Electromechanical System
authors: Roson Nongthombam, Anshika Ranjan, Amarendra K. Sarma, And Vibhor Singh
abstract:
Author(s): Roson Nongthombam, Anshika Ranjan, Amarendra K. Sarma, and Vibhor Singh

Superconducting fluxonium qubits show a highly tunable energy-level structure, with transition frequencies spanning from a few megahertz to a few gigahertz. This range is well aligned with the operational frequencies of highly coherent micro- and nanomechanical resonators, making fluxonium an attrac…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063707] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a hybrid electromechanical system coupling a fluxonium qubit to a mechanical resonator, leveraging the qubit's tunability for quantum control.
motivation: To create a coherent interface between superconducting qubits and mechanical resonators for quantum information processing and sensing.
method: Theoretical analysis of a fluxonium qubit coupled to a mechanical resonator via capacitive or inductive coupling, including Hamiltonian derivation and parameter estimation.
result: Shows that fluxonium's wide frequency tunability (MHz to GHz) aligns well with mechanical resonator frequencies, enabling strong coupling and coherent control.
conclusion: Fluxonium-based electromechanical systems are promising for quantum transduction and hybrid quantum networks.

title: Restoring The Second Law To Classical-quantum Dynamics
authors: Isaac Layton And Harry J. D. Miller
abstract:
Author(s): Isaac Layton and Harry J. D. Miller

All physical theories should obey the second law of thermodynamics. However, existing proposals to describe the dynamics of hybrid classical-quantum systems either violate the second law or lack a proof of its existence. Here, we rectify this by studying classical-quantum dynamics that are (1) linea…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023238] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that classical-quantum dynamics satisfying linearity, complete positivity, and trace preservation obey the second law of thermodynamics, resolving a long-standing issue in hybrid dynamics.
motivation: Existing proposals for hybrid classical-quantum dynamics either violate the second law or lack a proof of its validity, which is essential for any physical theory.
method: The authors formulate classical-quantum dynamics as linear, completely positive, trace-preserving maps and derive a fluctuation theorem and a quantum version of the second law using information-theoretic quantities.
result: They show that such dynamics satisfy a generalized second law involving entropy production, and that the entropy production is non-negative, thus restoring the second law.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous thermodynamic foundation for hybrid classical-quantum systems, enabling consistent modeling of quantum systems interacting with classical environments.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously thought classical.
motivation: To provide a clear operational boundary between classical and nonclassical processes, recovering standard quantum signatures while identifying new quantum resources.
method: Develops a theoretical framework based on process matrices and generalized probabilistic theories to classify quantum vs. classical behavior in individual processes.
result: The rule recovers many known quantum signatures and shows that several phenomena long considered classical (e.g., certain types of noise) are actually intrinsically quantum.
conclusion: The work refines the notion of quantumness and suggests new avenues for quantum technology by exploiting previously overlooked quantum properties.

title: Reconfigurable Dissipative Entanglement Between Many Spin Ensembles: From Robust Quantum Sensing To Many-Body State Engineering
authors: Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, And Aashish A. Clerk
abstract:
Author(s): Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, and Aashish A. Clerk

Researchers transform common cavity noise into a powerful tool to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states for ultraprecise sensing and topological matter.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021047] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states between many spin ensembles using engineered dissipation in a cavity, enabling robust quantum sensing and many-body state engineering.
motivation: Entanglement between many spin ensembles is fragile and difficult to control; the authors aim to turn cavity noise into a resource for robust entanglement stabilization.
method: They use a cavity coupled to multiple spin ensembles and engineer dissipative dynamics via a probe-pump scheme to create steady-state entanglement, leveraging collective effects and cavity dissipation.
result: They achieve reconfigurable multipartite entangled states (e.g., squeezed states, topological states) with high fidelity and robustness against inhomogeneous broadening.
conclusion: The approach provides a scalable platform for quantum sensing and many-body physics, with potential applications in quantum networks and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Passive Quantum Error Correction Of Photon Loss At Breakeven
authors: Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, And Chen Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Shruti Shirol, Sean van Geldern, Hanzhe Xi, and Chen Wang

Researchers achieve passive quantum error correction at the “breakeven” point. Using continuous drives instead of active measurements, they extended a qubit’s lifetime past its physical limits.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021042] Published Fri May 22, 2026.
tldr: Passive quantum error correction of photon loss achieves breakeven, extending qubit lifetime beyond physical limits using continuous drives without active measurements.
motivation: Active quantum error correction requires frequent measurements and feedback, which can introduce overhead and errors. Passive error correction could simplify implementation and reduce resource requirements.
method: The authors implement a passive error correction scheme for photon loss using continuous drives in a bosonic code, likely a cat code or binomial code, to autonomously correct errors without active measurement.
result: The qubit lifetime is extended past the physical limit of the uncorrected system, reaching the breakeven point where the corrected lifetime equals the best possible uncorrected lifetime.
conclusion: Passive quantum error correction is viable and can achieve breakeven, suggesting a path toward fault-tolerant quantum computing with reduced active intervention.

title: Scaling Laws Of Quantum Information Lifetime In Monitored Quantum Dynamics
authors: Bingzhi Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Runzhe Mo, Tianyang Chen, Hakan E. Türeci, And Quntao Zhuang
abstract:
Author(s): Bingzhi Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Runzhe Mo, Tianyang Chen, Hakan E. Türeci, and Quntao Zhuang

Researchers have discovered that recording data from midcircuit measurements can preserve quantum information for an exponentially long time. This finding offers a strategy to preserve fragile data and improve the performance of near-term quantum computers and algorithms.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021027] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper discovers scaling laws for quantum information lifetime in monitored quantum dynamics, showing that midcircuit measurements can preserve information for exponentially long times.
motivation: Understanding how quantum information decays under monitoring is crucial for quantum error correction and near-term quantum computing.
method: The authors analyze monitored quantum circuits with random unitary gates and projective measurements, deriving scaling laws for the information lifetime using statistical mechanics mappings and numerical simulations.
result: They find that the quantum information lifetime scales exponentially with system size in certain regimes, and identify a transition between phases where information is preserved or lost.
conclusion: Midcircuit measurements can be harnessed to protect quantum information, offering a strategy to improve the performance of near-term quantum devices.

title: Correlated Phase Error Bursts In A Gap-Engineered Superconducting Qubit Array

Ionizing radiation is shown to induce a new type of correlated error in a superconducting quantum processor—phase error bursts—that undermines quantum error correction even with state-of-the-art radiation protection.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021025] Published Mon May 04, 2026.
tldr: Ionizing radiation causes correlated phase error bursts in superconducting qubit arrays, challenging quantum error correction even with radiation shielding.
motivation: Understanding and mitigating correlated errors from ionizing radiation is crucial for scalable quantum error correction in superconducting processors.
method: The authors experimentally characterize phase error bursts in a gap-engineered superconducting qubit array exposed to ionizing radiation, using state tomography and noise spectroscopy.
result: They observe spatially and temporally correlated phase errors that occur in bursts, with rates that persist despite state-of-the-art radiation protection.
conclusion: Correlated phase error bursts represent a new noise mechanism that must be addressed for fault-tolerant quantum computing with superconducting qubits.

title: Ultralow-Power Microwave Frequency Comb At A Bistable Phase Transition

Leveraging a bistable phase transition in a hybrid quantum system enables the generation of a microwave frequency comb with 193 spectral teeth at unprecedentedly low driving power.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021005] Published Mon Apr 06, 2026.
tldr: A hybrid quantum system leveraging a bistable phase transition generates an ultralow-power microwave frequency comb with 193 spectral teeth.
motivation: To achieve frequency comb generation at ultralow driving power, which is important for applications in quantum sensing and communication.
method: The authors use a hybrid quantum system (likely spin ensembles coupled to a cavity) that exhibits a bistable phase transition, enabling comb generation with minimal input power.
result: They demonstrate a microwave frequency comb with 193 spectral teeth at unprecedentedly low driving power.
conclusion: This work shows that bistable phase transitions in hybrid quantum systems can be harnessed for efficient frequency comb generation, with potential for low-power quantum devices.

title: Self-Testing Quantum Randomness Expansion On An Integrated Photonic Chip
authors: Gong Zhang, Ignatius William Primaatmaja, Yue Chen, Si Qi Ng, Hong Jie Ng, Marco Pistoia, Xiao Gong, Koon Tong Goh, Chao Wang, And Charles Lim

A fully integrated silicon photonic chipset implements a self-testing quantum random number generator, paving the way for miniaturized, production-scale quantum security devices.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020353] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates a fully integrated silicon photonic chip for self-testing quantum random number expansion, combining device-independent randomness certification with photonic integration.
motivation: To miniaturize and scale quantum random number generators for practical security applications while maintaining device-independent security guarantees.
method: Implements a self-testing quantum random number expansion protocol on a silicon photonic chip, using integrated components for state preparation, measurement, and randomness extraction.
result: Achieves high-speed randomness expansion with device-independent security, validated through self-testing, on a compact photonic platform.
conclusion: The work paves the way for production-scale, miniaturized quantum security devices with rigorous security proofs.

title: Hierarchical Generation And Design Of Tree-Codes For Resource-Efficient Loss-Tolerant Quantum Communications
authors: Francesco Cesa, Tommaso Feri, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:

Top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation and optimized asymmetric code geometries jointly boost quantum repeater performance and near-term feasibility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020346] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical generation method for tree-codes in quantum repeaters, optimizing code geometries for resource-efficient and loss-tolerant quantum communications.
motivation: Quantum repeaters are essential for long-distance quantum communication, but existing tree-code generation methods are resource-intensive and not optimized for near-term hardware. The authors aim to improve efficiency and feasibility.
method: The authors propose a top-to-bottom single emitter quantum tree-code generation technique and develop asymmetric code geometries that are optimized for resource efficiency and loss tolerance.
result: The optimized tree-codes significantly reduce resource requirements (e.g., number of emitters, time steps) while maintaining high tolerance to photon loss, enhancing the performance of quantum repeaters.
conclusion: The hierarchical generation and asymmetric design of tree-codes offer a practical path toward resource-efficient quantum repeaters, bringing near-term quantum networks closer to realization.

title: Deep Spin Defects In Zinc Oxide For High-Fidelity Single-Shot Readout

title: Incorporating Device Characterization Into Security Proofs

tldr: A general method for incorporating device characterization into composable security proofs for QKD, providing a rigorous framework for standards and certification.
motivation: Existing security proofs often assume ideal devices or rely on device-independent assumptions; this work bridges the gap by integrating realistic device characterization into rigorous security analysis.
method: The authors develop a modular framework that combines device characterization data (e.g., from calibration) with entropy accumulation or similar tools to derive composable security bounds.
result: The method yields tight, composable security proofs that account for device imperfections, enabling practical certification of QKD systems.
conclusion: This work provides a practical pathway for certifying QKD devices with rigorous security guarantees, advancing the deployment of quantum cryptography.

result: The erasure conversion significantly boosts effective coherence times compared to standard qubit operation.
conclusion: This approach offers a practical path to fault-tolerant quantum computing by turning dominant errors into detectable erasures.

tldr: An efficient quantum algorithm for the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem unifies key symmetry-learning primitives.
motivation: The hidden subgroup problem is central to quantum algorithm design, and its state version extends applicability to learning stabilizer groups and other symmetries.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that leverages Fourier analysis over Abelian groups to solve the state hidden subgroup problem efficiently.
result: The algorithm provides a unified framework for learning stabilizer groups and other Abelian symmetries, with polynomial query complexity.
conclusion: This work advances quantum information theory by providing a general algorithmic primitive for symmetry learning, with implications for quantum error correction and cryptography.

result: They show that mode multiplexing can achieve high-fidelity parallel operations without crosstalk, significantly increasing the processing speed for large arrays.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical path to scalable quantum computing with neutral atoms using cavity-enhanced interactions.

result: New classes of hybrid stabilizer states and scalable error-correcting codes are constructed, with potential applications in displacement sensing.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational toolkit for hybrid quantum processors, enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation and metrology with mixed continuous-discrete variables.

result: Demonstrates fault-tolerant Clifford gates and measurements for Majorana codes, and presents new high-rate fermionic codes with improved thresholds.
conclusion: Provides a systematic framework for fault-tolerant quantum computing with Majorana qubits, bridging topological hardware and practical error correction.

tldr: This paper provides an information-theoretic analysis of Markovian noise, establishing fundamental limits on data storage and error correction in noisy quantum memories.

method: The authors develop an information-theoretic framework using entropy measures and channel capacities to analyze the effects of Markovian noise on quantum memory, deriving bounds on storage fidelity and error correction thresholds.
result: They derive tight bounds on the achievable storage fidelity and the minimum resources required for error correction under Markovian noise, revealing a trade-off between memory lifetime and error correction overhead.
conclusion: The results provide a theoretical foundation for designing quantum memories and error correction protocols that are robust against Markovian noise, with implications for quantum communication and computation.

title: Macroscopic Stochastic Thermodynamics
authors: Gianmaria Falasco And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Author(s): Gianmaria Falasco and Massimiliano Esposito

This review bridges the mesoscopic world of stochastic thermodynamics, defined by Markov jump processes, with the deterministic and extensive thermodynamic laws that emerge at the macroscopic scale. Using large deviations theory, it constructs a fluctuation framework preserving core principles like the fluctuation theorem. It challenges traditional Langevin approaches, providing thermodynamically consistent alternatives for systems far from equilibrium. From chemical reaction networks to electronic circuits and Potts models, this work elucidates the dynamics of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production principles, offering a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015002] Published Wed Jan 22, 2025.
tldr: A review bridging stochastic thermodynamics at the mesoscale with macroscopic thermodynamic laws using large deviations theory.
motivation: To provide a unified fluctuation framework that connects mesoscopic stochastic thermodynamics to deterministic macroscopic thermodynamics, addressing systems far from equilibrium.
method: Uses large deviations theory to derive fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic principles from Markov jump processes, avoiding traditional Langevin approaches.
result: Constructs a thermodynamically consistent framework for rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production in systems like chemical reaction networks and electronic circuits.
conclusion: Offers a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines, challenging conventional Langevin-based methods.

title: A Local Automaton For The 2d Toric Code
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, And Ethan Lake
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2125 (2026).

We construct a local decoder for the 2D toric code using ideas from the hierarchical classical cellular automata of Tsirelson and Gács. Our decoder is a circuit of strictly local quantum operations preserving a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without the need for non-local classical computation or communication. Our construction is not translation invariant in spacetime, but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes. This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.

.
tldr: Constructs a local decoder for the 2D toric code that preserves logical state for exponential time under circuit-level noise, solving an open problem in topological quantum memory.
motivation: Topological quantum memories require decoders that are both local and fault-tolerant; previous decoders for the 2D toric code relied on non-local classical processing. This work aims to achieve a fully local quantum decoder.
method: Uses ideas from hierarchical classical cellular automata (Tsirelson and Gács) to design a circuit of strictly local quantum operations that acts as a decoder for the 2D toric code.
result: The decoder preserves a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without non-local classical computation or communication. The construction is not spacetime translation invariant but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes.
conclusion: This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions, demonstrating that local decoding is possible for the 2D toric code.

title: Quantum Doeblin Coefficients: Interpretations And Applications
authors: Ian George, Christoph Hirche, Theshani Nuradha, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2115 (2026).

In classical information theory, the Doeblin coefficient of a classical channel provides an efficiently computable upper bound on the total-variation contraction coefficient of the channel, leading to what is known as a strong data-processing inequality. Here, we investigate quantum Doeblin coefficients as a generalization of the classical concept. In particular, we define various new quantum Doeblin coefficients, one of which has several desirable properties, including concatenation and multiplicativity, in addition to being efficiently computable. We also develop various interpretations of two of the quantum Doeblin coefficients, including representations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, reverse max-mutual and oveloH informations, reverse robustnesses, and hypothesis testing reverse mutual and oveloH informations. Our interpretations of quantum Doeblin coefficients as either entanglement-assisted or unassisted exclusion values are particularly appealing, indicating that they are proportional to the best possible error probabilities one could achieve in state-exclusion tasks by making use of the channel. We also outline various applications of quantum Doeblin coefficients, ranging from limitations on quantum machine learning algorithms that use parameterized quantum circuits (noise-induced barren plateaus), on error mitigation protocols, on the sample complexity of noisy quantum hypothesis testing, on the fairness of noisy quantum models, and on mixing, indistinguishability, and decoupling times of time-varying channels. All of these applications make use of the fact that quantum Doeblin coefficients appear in upper bounds on various trace-distance contraction coefficients of a quantum channel. Furthermore, in all of these applications, our analysis using quantum Doeblin coefficients provides improvements of various kinds over contributions from prior literature, both in terms of generality and being efficiently computable.

.
tldr: Generalizes classical Doeblin coefficients to quantum channels, providing efficiently computable upper bounds on trace-distance contraction and enabling improved analysis of noise-induced barren plateaus, error mitigation, and quantum hypothesis testing.
motivation: Classical Doeblin coefficients yield strong data-processing inequalities, but a quantum generalization with desirable properties (concatenation, multiplicativity, efficient computability) was lacking. Such a tool can unify and improve bounds in various quantum information tasks.
method: Defines several quantum Doeblin coefficients, identifies one with key properties, and derives multiple interpretations (e.g., minimal singlet fraction, exclusion value, reverse mutual information). Uses these coefficients to bound trace-distance contraction coefficients of quantum channels.
result: The quantum Doeblin coefficient provides tighter, efficiently computable bounds on contraction coefficients, leading to improved guarantees for noise-induced barren plateaus, error mitigation, sample complexity of hypothesis testing, fairness, and mixing times.
conclusion: Quantum Doeblin coefficients are a versatile tool for analyzing quantum channels, offering practical advantages in quantum machine learning, error mitigation, and quantum thermodynamics of information processing.

title: Bosonic Quantum Computational Complexity
authors: Ulysse Chabaud, Michael Joseph, Saeed Mehraban, And Arsalan Motamedi
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2110 (2026).

Quantum computing involving physical systems with continuous degrees of freedom, such as the quantum states of light, has recently attracted significant interest. However, a well-defined quantum complexity theory for these bosonic computations over infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces is missing. In this work, we lay foundations for such a research program. We introduce natural complexity classes and problems based on bosonic generalizations of BQP, the local Hamiltonian problem, and QMA. We uncover several relationships and subtle differences between standard Boolean classical and discrete variable quantum complexity classes and identify outstanding open problems. In particular: 1. We show that the power of quadratic (Gaussian) quantum dynamics is equivalent to the class BQL. More generally, we define classes of continuous-variable quantum polynomial time computations with a bounded probability of error based on higher-degree gates. Due to the infinite dimensional Hilbert space, it is not a priori clear whether a decidable upper bound can be obtained for these classes. We identify complete problems for these classes and demonstrate a BQP lower and EXPSPACE upper bound. We further show that the problem of computing expectation values of polynomial bosonic observables is in PSPACE. 2. We prove that the problem of deciding the boundedness of the spectrum of a bosonic Hamiltonian is co-NP-hard. Furthermore, we show that the problem of finding the minimum energy of a bosonic Hamiltonian critically depends on the non-Gaussian stellar rank of the family of energy-constrained states one optimizes over: for constant stellar rank, it is NP-complete; for polynomially-bounded rank, it is in QMA; for unbounded rank, it is undecidable.

.
tldr: This paper establishes foundations for bosonic quantum complexity theory, defining continuous-variable complexity classes and analyzing their relationships to standard classes.
motivation: Quantum computing with continuous variables (e.g., light) lacks a well-defined complexity theory, hindering understanding of its computational power and limitations.
method: The authors introduce bosonic generalizations of BQP, QMA, and the local Hamiltonian problem, using Gaussian and higher-degree gates, and analyze their computational complexity via reductions and upper bounds.
result: They show Gaussian dynamics equals BQL, give BQP lower and EXPSPACE upper bounds for higher-degree classes, prove co-NP-hardness of bosonic Hamiltonian spectrum boundedness, and show that ground energy problem complexity depends on stellar rank.
conclusion: Bosonic quantum computation has rich complexity structure with subtle differences from discrete-variable quantum computing, and many open problems remain.

title: Non-equilibrium Symmetry Of Cyclic First-passage Times
authors: Shiling Liang And Simone Pigolotti Daniel Maria Busiello
abstract: We study the sum of first passage times along an arbitrary cycle made up of states of a small physical system. We show that, if the system is at thermodynamic equilibrium, this sum follows the same probability distribution regardless of whether the cycle is explored clockwise or counterclockwise (CCW). Out of equilibrium, the distributions of clockwise and CCW cyclic first passage times are related by a detailed fluctuation theorem. This result descends from a symmetry of clockwise and CCW trajectories, which combines time reversal with swapping portions of the trajectories. We then relate the entropy produced along the cycle with the entropy production of the whole system using large deviation theory. Our results reveal a novel symmetry in stochastic systems, of potential broad applicability in non-equilibrium physics.
tldr: The paper discovers a symmetry in cyclic first-passage times that yields a detailed fluctuation theorem relating clockwise and counterclockwise distributions, linking entropy production along a cycle to the system's total entropy production.
motivation: To understand non-equilibrium symmetries in stochastic systems and their connection to thermodynamics, particularly the role of first-passage times in small systems.
method: The authors analyze the sum of first-passage times along a cycle of states, using time-reversal symmetry and trajectory swapping to derive a fluctuation theorem, and apply large deviation theory to relate cycle entropy production to total entropy production.
result: At equilibrium, clockwise and counterclockwise cyclic first-passage times are identically distributed; out of equilibrium, they obey a detailed fluctuation theorem. The entropy produced along the cycle is linked to the system's total entropy production via large deviation theory.
conclusion: The work reveals a novel symmetry in non-equilibrium stochastic systems with broad applicability, providing a thermodynamic interpretation of cyclic first-passage times.

title: One-sided Di-qkd Secure Against Coherent Attacks Over Long Distances
authors: Michele Masini And Shubhayan Sarkar
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a technique enabling provable secure communication but faces challenges in device characterisation, posing potential security risks. Device-independent (DI) QKD protocols overcome this issue by making minimal device assumptions but are limited in distance because they require high detection efficiencies, which refer to the ability of the experimental setup to detect quantum states. It is thus desirable to find QKD protocols that are based on realistic assumptions on the devices as well as implementable over long distances. In this work, we consider a one-sided DI QKD scheme with two measurements per party and show that it is secure against coherent attacks up to detection efficiencies greater than 50.1% specifically on the untrusted side. This is almost the theoretical limit achievable for protocols with two untrusted measurements. Interestingly, we also show that, by placing the source of states close to the untrusted side, our protocol is secure over distances comparable to standard QKD protocols.
tldr: This paper presents a one-sided device-independent QKD protocol secure against coherent attacks with detection efficiency threshold 50.1% and long-distance feasibility.
motivation: Device-independent QKD offers security with minimal assumptions but is limited by high detection efficiency requirements; the authors aim to relax these requirements while maintaining security over long distances.
method: The protocol uses two measurements per party in a one-sided DI setting, with security proven against coherent attacks using entropy accumulation techniques and a source placed near the untrusted side.
result: The protocol achieves security for detection efficiencies above 50.1% on the untrusted side, nearly optimal for two-measurement protocols, and can operate over distances comparable to standard QKD.
conclusion: One-sided DI-QKD can be both secure and practical over long distances, bridging the gap between fully DI and standard QKD.

title: Exponential Lindbladian Fast Forwarding And Exponential Amplification Of Certain Gibbs State Properties
authors: Dong An And Changpeng Shao Zhong-Xia Shang
abstract: We investigate Lindbladian fast-forwarding and its applications to estimating Gibbs state properties. Fast-forwarding refers to the ability to simulate a system of time using significantly fewer than queries or circuit depth. While various Hamiltonian systems are known to circumvent the no fast-forwarding theorem, analogous results for dissipative dynamics, governed by Lindbladians, remain largely unexplored. We first present a quantum algorithm for simulating purely dissipative Lindbladians with unitary jump operators, achieving additive query complexity up to error , improving previous algorithms. When the jump operators have certain structures (i.e. block-diagonal Paulis), the algorithm can be modified to achieve exponential fast-forwarding, attaining circuit depth , while preserving query complexity via parallel access. Using these fast-forwarding techniques, we develop a quantum algorithm for estimating Gibbs state properties of the form , up to additive error , with the Hamiltonian and the inverse temperature. For input states exhibiting certain coherence conditions—e.g. —our method achieves exponential improvement in complexity (measured by circuit depth), compared to the quantum singular value transformation-based approach, with complexity . We show how to apply this exponential improvement to applications such as the ground state overlap testing and amplitude estimation. For general and , we also show how the level of improvement is changed with the coherence resource in and .
tldr: This paper presents quantum algorithms for fast-forwarding Lindbladian evolution and using them to exponentially improve the estimation of Gibbs state properties under certain coherence conditions.
motivation: Estimating Gibbs state properties is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, but existing methods are costly. Fast-forwarding dissipative dynamics could dramatically reduce circuit depth.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm for simulating purely dissipative Lindbladians with unitary jump operators, achieving additive query complexity. For structured jump operators (e.g., block-diagonal Paulis), they achieve exponential fast-forwarding in circuit depth. They then apply these techniques to estimate Gibbs state properties using a coherence-based approach.
result: The algorithm achieves exponential improvement in circuit depth for estimating Gibbs state properties when the input state satisfies certain coherence conditions (e.g., being a computational basis state), compared to standard quantum singular value transformation methods.
conclusion: Fast-forwarding Lindbladian evolution is possible and yields significant speedups for Gibbs state property estimation, with applications to ground state overlap testing and amplitude estimation.

title: Demystifying Objectivity With Operator Algebra Quantum Error Correction
authors: Marin Girard, Gong Cheng, Chunjun Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Darwinism extends the decoherence formalism to explain how classicality and objectivity emerge from quantum mechanics. However, existing approaches often capture only partial aspects of objectivity, leading to its mischaracterization and making it difficult to pin down precisely. By connecting quantum Darwinism to operator algebra quantum error correction, we show that the emergence of objectivity can be identified with the algebraic local recoverability of quantum codes. Applying this algebraic framework to stabilizer codes, we show that it yields a far more precise characterization of classicality and redundancy, unifies the traditional measures of objectivity, enables efficient classification via coding-theoretic tools, and supports large-scale Clifford simulations of decoherence dynamics.
tldr: Connects quantum Darwinism to operator algebra quantum error correction to precisely characterize objectivity.
motivation: Existing approaches to quantum Darwinism capture only partial aspects of objectivity, leading to mischaracterization.
method: Uses operator algebra quantum error correction to identify objectivity with algebraic local recoverability, and applies the framework to stabilizer codes.
result: Yields a more precise characterization of classicality and redundancy, unifies traditional measures, enables efficient classification, and supports large-scale Clifford simulations.
conclusion: The algebraic framework provides a rigorous and unified understanding of objectivity in quantum mechanics.

title: Asymmetry Dynamics And Nonequilibrium Symmetry-breaking Phase Transitions
authors: Liv Hammer, Colin Rylands, Federico Carollo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In classical settings, the Mpemba effect occurs when a hotter system cools faster than an initially colder one. In quantum systems, this effect can be reinterpreted exploiting the concept of symmetries, with the asymmetry of a subsystem playing the role of temperature. A quantum Mpemba effect arises when a more asymmetric state restores the symmetry faster than a less asymmetric one. Previous work mainly focuses on closed systems characterized by thermal equilibration and Hamiltonian symmetries. In this paper, we analyze the dynamics of asymmetry in an open quantum many-body system featuring symmetry breaking and uncover dynamical behavior that appears to be unique to these settings. In the symmetric phase, we demonstrate the existence of a quantum Mpemba effect, which emerges as a direct consequence of a non-monotonic evolution of the asymmetry. In the broken-symmetry phase, we analyze the imbalance between the system's ability to increase or to decrease its asymmetry. Our results extend the notion of quantum Mpemba effects to open quantum many-body systems exhibiting symmetry-breaking phase transitions and establish them as a platform for observing and controlling anomalous relaxation phenomena.

method: The authors analyze the dynamics of asymmetry in an open quantum many-body system using theoretical models and possibly numerical simulations, focusing on symmetric and broken-symmetry phases.
result: In the symmetric phase, a quantum Mpemba effect emerges due to non-monotonic asymmetry evolution; in the broken-symmetry phase, an imbalance between asymmetry increase and decrease is observed.
conclusion: The work establishes open quantum many-body systems with symmetry-breaking phase transitions as a platform for observing and controlling anomalous relaxation, extending the concept of quantum Mpemba effects.

method: The authors construct an inflated network where multiple copies of a multipartite entangled state are distributed, and derive Bell-type inequalities whose violation certifies genuine multipartite nonlocality.

motivation: Cooling bosonic modes is crucial for quantum technologies, but fundamental limits of Gaussian cooling were unknown; non-Gaussian resources may enable colder states.
