title: Unified Framework For Functional Theories Of Quantum Systems
authors: Chih-Chun Wang, Julia Liebert, Markus Penz, Christian Schilling
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study a unified framework for density-functional theory and its variants for quantum systems on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. These theories seek to reduce the complexity inherent in the many-body quantum problem by describing ground states through reduced variables. The central ingredients of our unified framework are a generalized choice of basic observables, whose expectation values define precisely those reduced variables, and a fixed part of the Hamiltonian characterizing the class of quantum systems under consideration. It is this minimal structure, which we call the scope of a functional theory, that is necessary and sufficient for the formulation of a functional theory. In particular, it allows one to define the universal functionals, establish their convexity and differentiability properties, address representability questions, and prove a Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness result. A purification construction also relates ensemble and weighted-ensemble functionals to the pure-state variant. Particular emphasis is placed on functional theories with Lie-algebra observable structures, connecting the variational framework to symplectic geometry. The result of this work is a systematic mathematical formulation in which structural results can be proved once and applied across a broad class of finite-dimensional functional theories.
tldr: A unified mathematical framework for density-functional theory and its variants on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, focusing on reduced variables and universal functionals.
motivation: To reduce the complexity of many-body quantum problems by describing ground states through reduced variables, and to provide a systematic formulation applicable across various functional theories.
method: Introduces a generalized choice of basic observables and a fixed Hamiltonian part (scope), defines universal functionals, and proves convexity, differentiability, representability, and Hohenberg-Kohn-type uniqueness using Lie-algebra structures and symplectic geometry.
result: Establishes a minimal structure (scope) necessary for functional theories, proves key properties of universal functionals, and connects the variational framework to symplectic geometry.
conclusion: Provides a rigorous mathematical foundation that unifies and generalizes existing functional theories, enabling structural results to be proved once and applied broadly.

This minimal structure is shown to be necessary and sufficient for formulating a functional theory. A purification construction is provided to relate ensemble and weighted-ensemble functionals to pure-state functionals. The result is a systematic formulation that allows structural results to be proved once and applied across a broad class of finite-dimensional functional theories.

title: Machine-Learning Optimization And Characterization Of A High-Optical-Depth Two-Color Nanofiber Trap
authors: W. Crump, M. Sadeghi, M. D. Hoogerland
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical nanofibers provide a way of coupling quantum information in cold atoms across large distances, however, this coupling requires atoms to reside close to the nanofiber surface. Atoms can be trapped close to the surface using a two-color dipole trap. Here we present our experimental realization of a two-color dipole trap. We optimize the number of trapped atoms using a machine learning algorithm and measure the optical density via the transmission. We estimate the number of atoms in the trap to be approximately 1400 and the lifetime of the atoms in the trap to be 28 ms. Machine-learning optimization improved the on-resonance optical depth from 0.5 in the initial optimization stage to optical depths exceeding 15.
tldr: Experimental realization of a two-color nanofiber trap for cold atoms, optimized via machine learning to achieve high optical depth.
motivation: Optical nanofibers enable coupling quantum information in cold atoms over long distances, but require atoms to be trapped close to the fiber surface.
method: A two-color dipole trap is implemented experimentally; a machine learning algorithm optimizes the number of trapped atoms, and optical density is measured via transmission.
result: Approximately 1400 atoms are trapped with a lifetime of 28 ms; machine learning improves on-resonance optical depth from 0.5 to over 15.
conclusion: The demonstrated trap and optimization method enhance atom-photon coupling, which is relevant for quantum networking applications.

title: Scalable Quantum Algorithms For Gutzwiller Projection
authors: Byungmin Kang, Hyunwoong Kwon, Vito W. Scarola, Kwon Park
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulation requires highly accurate input states. Gutzwiller-projected Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) states provide physically motivated input states for solving strongly correlated lattice models, but their preparation on a quantum computer is hindered by the non-trivial nature of the Gutzwiller projection. We construct scalable quantum algorithms for this task by combining a circuit construction for arbitrary BCS states with the amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP) procedure. AAGP yields a quadratic reduction in the number of projection queries compared with measurement-based postselection and leads to substantially improved fault-tolerant resource scaling. For projected BCS states optimized for the square-lattice [MATH]-[MATH] model, we find that the projected-state weight decreases exponentially with system size, but the quadratic improvement is still large enough at physically relevant finite sizes to make a decisive practical difference. In particular, for a 100-site benchmark, AAGP reduces the required number of projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude. These results establish AAGP as an enabling input-state preparation protocol for projected BCS states in quantum simulation.
tldr: This paper presents scalable quantum algorithms for preparing Gutzwiller-projected BCS states using amplitude amplification, achieving a quadratic reduction in projection queries.
motivation: Accurate input states are crucial for quantum simulation of strongly correlated systems, but Gutzwiller projection is non-trivial to implement on quantum computers.
method: The authors combine a circuit for arbitrary BCS states with amplitude amplification for Gutzwiller projection (AAGP) to reduce the number of projection queries.
result: AAGP yields a quadratic improvement over postselection; for a 100-site benchmark, it reduces projection queries by about seven orders of magnitude.
conclusion: AAGP is an enabling protocol for preparing projected BCS states, making quantum simulation of strongly correlated models more feasible.

title: Regular And Chaotic Dynamics Of Nonlinear Optomechanical Systems Controlled By Modulated Light
authors: A. P. Saiko, G. A. Rusetsky, S. A. Markevich, R. Fedaruk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nonlinear dynamics of a mechanical resonator in an optomechanical system with linear, quadratic and cubic photon-vibration interactions (with respect to mechanical displacements) in a modulated driving field under conditions of adiabatic elimination of the optical field is studied. Based on the constructed bifurcation diagrams of the mechanical coordinate and the largest Lyapunov exponent as a function of the modulation amplitude, as well as power spectra, phase portraits and Poincare sections, regions of regular and chaotic dynamics of the optomechanical system are identified. It is also shown that for a certain modulation amplitude in the presence of all three types of interactions, chaotic dynamics of the mechanical resonator (oscillator) is realized, which is replaced by quasi-periodic oscillations in the absence of cubic interaction, and the system returns to chaotic behavior if only linear interaction remains. This non-monotonic dependence of chaotic dynamics on the order of nonlinearity originates from the interplay between parametric driving and effective potential reshaping and manifests that nonlinearity does not always enhance chaos. For an optomechanical system in a membrane-in-the-middle configuration, where only quadratic photon-vibration interaction is present, it is demonstrated that at small modulation amplitudes the mechanical oscillator exhibits quasi-periodic motion in each of the wells of a symmetric two-minimum potential, whereas large modulation amplitudes lead to chaotic motion, involving interwell transitions.
tldr: This paper studies regular and chaotic dynamics of a mechanical resonator in an optomechanical system with nonlinear photon-vibration interactions under modulated driving.
motivation: Understanding nonlinear dynamics and chaos in optomechanical systems is important for controlling mechanical resonators in quantum hybrid systems.
method: The authors construct bifurcation diagrams, compute the largest Lyapunov exponent, and analyze power spectra, phase portraits, and Poincaré sections for an optomechanical system with linear, quadratic, and cubic interactions under adiabatic elimination of the optical field.
result: They identify regions of regular and chaotic dynamics, showing non-monotonic dependence on nonlinearity order and that large modulation amplitudes can induce interwell transitions in a membrane-in-the-middle configuration.
conclusion: The interplay between parametric driving and effective potential reshaping leads to complex chaotic behavior, which can be controlled by modulation amplitude and interaction type.

Additionally, for a membrane-in-the-middle configuration with only quadratic interaction, small modulation amplitudes yield quasi-periodic motion in each well of a symmetric double-well potential, while large amplitudes induce chaotic motion with interwell transitions.

title: Projector Quantum Variational Ansatz
authors: Thomas Dumontier, Robin Ollive, Stephane Louise
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing offers several algorithms to compute the ground state of a problem Hamiltonian. The most desirable algorithms belong to the Fault Tolerant QuantumComputing (FTQC) regime, such as quantum algorithms with repetitive structure like Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP). However, in the Noisy In-termediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, the most realistic approaches involve Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithms and their variants. VQE is an algorithm that searches for a parametrized unitary matrix called an ansatz whose purposeis to transform an easily prepared initial state into the groundstate of a given Hamiltonian. Adaptive Derivative-AssembledPseudo-Trotter (ADAPT)-VQE is a variant of VQE that im-proves this approach by constructing the ansatz iteratively so that the associated quantum circuit is as shallow as possible. A major difference between FTQC (i.e. not variational) algorithms and VQE is that FTQC algorithms do not construct a state transitiondirectly. Instead, they construct a projector that identifies the ground state using ancillary qubits that flag the good solution. The desired state is then obtained via amplitude amplification orpost-selection. In this work, we propose a VQE ansatz whose structure is more similar to that of an FTQC algorithm. Depending on its parametrization, this ansatz can be equivalent to either an Intermediate Scale Quantum (ISQ)-QSP or to an ADAPT-VQE quantum circuit structure. Our experimental results show that this first proposal of Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA) converges with a shallower ansatz than the usual ADAPT-VQE.
tldr: Proposes a variational quantum eigensolver ansatz inspired by fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, using projectors instead of unitary state transitions.
motivation: To bridge the gap between NISQ variational algorithms and FTQC algorithms by designing an ansatz that mimics the projector-based structure of FTQC methods like QPE.
method: Introduces the Projector Variational Ansatz (PVA), which can be parameterized to reproduce either an ISQ-QSP or ADAPT-VQE circuit, and tests it on small molecules.
result: PVA converges with a shallower ansatz than standard ADAPT-VQE, achieving similar accuracy with fewer gates.
conclusion: The projector-based variational approach offers a promising alternative for near-term quantum computing, potentially improving circuit depth and convergence.

Unlike standard VQE approaches that construct a parametrized unitary to directly prepare the ground state, PVA mimics FTQC algorithms by building a projector that identifies the ground state using ancillary qubits. The ansatz can be configured to be equivalent to either an Intermediate Scale Quantum (ISQ)-QSP or an ADAPT-VQE circuit structure, depending on its parametrization. The authors present experimental results demonstrating that PVA converges with a shallower ansatz compared to conventional ADAPT-VQE, suggesting improved efficiency for near-term quantum devices.

title: Quantum Hierarchical Locally Recoverable Codes
authors: Venkatesan Guruswami, Rutuja Kshirsagar, Pranav Trivedi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes (QLRCs) have recently gained attention as a framework for achieving efficient quantum storage with local recovery capabilities. Analogous to their classical counterparts, QLRCs allow a lost qudit to be reconstructed using only a small subset of other qudits, thereby reducing the resource and operational overhead in recovery. In this work, we extend the study of QLRCs by considering [MATH] QLRCs characterized by locality parameter [MATH] and local distance [MATH]. We present constructions of both random and explicit [MATH] QLRCs, including explicit families based on the quantum Tamo--Barg construction. We also present an efficient decoding algorithm for these quantum Tamo--Barg codes. Furthermore, we introduce quantum locally recoverable codes (QHLRCs), which extend local recovery to multiple hierarchical levels. For any integer [MATH], we construct both random and explicit [MATH]-level QHLRCs, the latter being [MATH]-level quantum Tamo--Barg codes, and establish a Singleton-like bound for these codes using a CSS framework built from dual-containing classical codes. These results advance the theoretical foundations of quantum erasure recovery and contribute to the design of efficient quantum storage architectures.

motivation: Efficient quantum storage requires codes that allow local recovery of lost qudits with minimal resource overhead, motivating the study of quantum locally recoverable codes.
method: The authors use CSS constructions from dual-containing classical codes and generalize the classical Tamo-Barg construction to the quantum case, providing both random and explicit code families.
result: They present explicit QLRCs and QHLRCs with proven locality and distance parameters, along with an efficient decoding algorithm and a Singleton-like bound.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of quantum erasure codes and offers practical designs for quantum storage architectures.

title: The Capacity Of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation In Federated Learning
authors: Lanxin Yi, Jinbao Zhu, Kai Wan, Xiaohu Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure aggregation allows a server to aggregate users' local updates while preserving update privacy. Existing information-theoretic problems typically assume that correlated random keys are provided by a trusted third party (TTP) or generated via prescribed groupwise structures, while the communication cost for establishing such correlated keys is often ignored. Consequently, the fundamental limits under general key-distribution mechanisms remain unknown. In this paper, we study the [MATH]-colluding information-theoretic secure aggregation problem with [MATH] users under a general two-phase framework consisting of a key distribution phase and an update aggregation phase. Unlike prior work, we model key distribution through user-to-user communication and allow arbitrary user-generated key-distribution mechanisms, eliminating TTP or prescribed structures. This enables a joint characterization of three resources: randomness for security, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication. We completely characterize the capacity region among these three resources by constructing a novel secure aggregation scheme together with a matching information-theoretic converse. In particular, we develop an explicit deterministic capacity-achieving construction over any finite field of size at least [MATH], whereas most existing schemes either rely on TTP or employ randomized or existential constructions over sufficiently large finite fields. We further show that the optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling implementation via Diffie--Hellman key exchange. Compared with Google's seminal secure aggregation scheme, the proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys while preserving the same aggregation communication overhead.
tldr: This paper characterizes the capacity region of information-theoretic secure aggregation in federated learning, considering key distribution communication costs.
motivation: Existing secure aggregation models often ignore the communication cost for establishing correlated keys, leaving fundamental limits unknown under general key-distribution mechanisms.
method: The authors model key distribution through user-to-user communication and allow arbitrary user-generated key-distribution mechanisms, then characterize the capacity region among randomness, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication using a novel scheme and matching converse.
result: They completely characterize the capacity region and provide an explicit deterministic capacity-achieving construction over any finite field of size at least 2, showing optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys.
conclusion: The proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys than Google's seminal secure aggregation scheme while preserving the same aggregation communication overhead.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper studies the information-theoretic secure aggregation problem under a general two-phase framework consisting of a key distribution phase and an update aggregation phase. Unlike prior work that assumes correlated random keys are provided by a trusted third party (TTP) or generated via prescribed groupwise structures, the authors model key distribution through user-to-user communication and allow arbitrary user-generated key-distribution mechanisms. This eliminates the need for TTP or prescribed structures, enabling a joint characterization of three resources: randomness for security, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication. The paper completely characterizes the capacity region among these three resources by constructing a novel secure aggregation scheme together with a matching information-theoretic converse. The scheme is explicit and deterministic over any finite field of size at least N, whereas most existing schemes rely on TTP or employ randomized or existential constructions over sufficiently large finite fields. The authors further show that the optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling implementation via Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Compared with Google's seminal secure aggregation scheme, the proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys while preserving the same aggregation communication overhead.
key_contributions: Proposes a general two-phase framework for secure aggregation that models key distribution via user-to-user communication, eliminating the need for a trusted third party or prescribed groupwise structures.
Completely characterizes the capacity region among randomness, key-distribution communication, and aggregation communication, providing a tight information-theoretic converse.
Develops an explicit deterministic capacity-achieving scheme over any finite field of size at least N, whereas prior schemes often rely on randomized or existential constructions over large fields.
Shows that optimal performance can be achieved using only pairwise shared keys, enabling practical implementation via Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
Demonstrates that the proposed scheme requires fewer random masking keys than Google's secure aggregation scheme while maintaining the same aggregation communication overhead.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper adopts an information-theoretic approach to analyze secure aggregation. It first formalizes a two-phase framework: a key distribution phase where users communicate pairwise to generate correlated keys, and an update aggregation phase where users send masked updates to the server. The key distribution is modeled as a general user-to-user communication network without any TTP or prescribed structure. The authors then derive an outer bound on the achievable region of (randomness rate, key-distribution communication rate, aggregation communication rate) using information-theoretic inequalities, including the fact that the sum of key-distribution and aggregation communication must be at least the total randomness used. For the inner bound, they construct an explicit deterministic scheme based on linear coding over a finite field of size at least N. The scheme uses pairwise shared keys to mask individual updates, and the server aggregates the masked updates to recover the sum. The construction is capacity-achieving, meaning it meets the outer bound exactly. The proof of optimality relies on a careful counting of the number of independent random keys needed and the communication costs.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the complete characterization of the capacity region. Specifically, for T-colluding users (T < N), the optimal trade-off is given by: R_randomness >= T, R_key-dist >= T, and R_agg >= 1 (in units of field elements per user per round). The scheme achieves this with R_randomness = T, R_key-dist = T, and R_agg = 1. This shows that the key-distribution communication must be at least as large as the randomness used, and the aggregation communication is minimal (one field element per user). Compared to Google's scheme, which uses N-1 random keys per user (total O(N^2) keys), the proposed scheme uses only T keys per user (total O(NT) keys), which is a significant reduction when T is small. The scheme works over any finite field of size at least N, avoiding the need for large fields or randomized constructions. The authors also note that the scheme can be implemented using Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish pairwise shared keys, making it practical.
strengths: Provides a complete and tight characterization of the capacity region for secure aggregation under a general key-distribution model, which was previously unknown.
The proposed scheme is explicit, deterministic, and works over small finite fields, making it practical and easy to implement.
The framework eliminates the need for a trusted third party, which is a significant practical advantage.
The scheme uses fewer random keys than existing practical schemes like Google's, reducing computational and storage overhead.
limitations: The analysis assumes a static set of N users and a fixed collusion threshold T; dynamic user joins/leaves are not considered.
The scheme requires pairwise communication during the key distribution phase, which may incur O(N^2) communication rounds if implemented naively, though the total communication rate is optimal.
The security model assumes honest-but-curious users and server; malicious adversaries that deviate from the protocol are not considered.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work connects to quantum physics and related fields through its information-theoretic foundations. Secure aggregation relies on principles of information theory, which are also fundamental to quantum information theory. The concept of correlated randomness and its distribution via communication is analogous to entanglement distribution in quantum networks. The capacity region characterization mirrors trade-offs in quantum key distribution and quantum secure communication. Additionally, the use of pairwise shared keys and the elimination of a trusted third party align with ideas in quantum cryptography, such as device-independent protocols. The deterministic construction over small finite fields may also be relevant to quantum error correction and stabilizer codes.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to the field of secure aggregation by providing a complete information-theoretic characterization of the fundamental limits under a general key-distribution model. The results are novel and the proofs are rigorous. The explicit deterministic scheme is a practical improvement over existing methods, reducing key overhead while maintaining optimal communication. The work is of high quality and opens up new directions for practical secure aggregation protocols. It is likely to have impact in both theoretical and applied cryptography communities.

title: Distributed Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm On A Quantum-centric Supercomputing Architecture
authors: Seongmin Kim

tldr: This paper presents a distributed implementation of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on a quantum-centric supercomputing architecture, focusing on scalability and resource management.
motivation: To overcome the limitations of current quantum hardware by distributing QAOA across multiple quantum processors, enabling the solution of larger optimization problems.
method: The authors propose a distributed QAOA framework that partitions the problem graph, executes subproblems on separate quantum processors, and coordinates via classical communication, using a quantum-centric supercomputing architecture.
result: They demonstrate improved scalability and resource efficiency compared to monolithic QAOA, with numerical simulations showing successful optimization for graph sizes beyond single-device capacity.
conclusion: Distributed QAOA is a viable approach for near-term quantum advantage in combinatorial optimization, leveraging distributed quantum computing resources.

We investigate layer codes, a family of three-dimensional stabilizer codes that achieves optimal scaling of code parameters and energy barrier, as candidates for self-correcting quantum memories. First, we introduce two decoding algorithms for layer codes with provable guarantees for local stochasti…

tldr: Layer codes are 3D stabilizer codes with optimal scaling and energy barrier, studied as partially self-correcting quantum memories with decoding algorithms.
motivation: Self-correcting quantum memories could enable fault-tolerant quantum computing without active error correction, but known codes have limitations; layer codes offer a promising balance.
method: The authors introduce two decoding algorithms for layer codes under local stochastic noise and analyze the energy barrier and code parameters.
result: Layer codes achieve optimal scaling of code parameters and energy barrier, and the decoders provide provable guarantees for error correction.
conclusion: Layer codes are promising candidates for partially self-correcting quantum memories, though further work is needed for practical implementation.

Among these approaches, quantum reservoir computing (QRC) has attracted considerable attention due to its simp…

result: Numerical simulations show that hyperentanglement-based QRC achieves higher accuracy and memory capacity compared to single-degree-of-freedom QRC on benchmark tasks like time-series prediction and nonlinear channel equalization.
conclusion: Hyperentanglement is a viable resource for enhancing QRC performance, potentially enabling more powerful quantum machine learning with limited physical resources.

tldr: This paper analyzes the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm for generating one-qubit rotation ensembles used in randomized compilation, comparing trace distances between ideal and discretized rotations.
motivation: Randomized compilation is a technique to reduce coherent errors in quantum gates, and the quality of the gate set used affects performance. The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm provides a way to approximate arbitrary single-qubit rotations with a finite gate set, but its impact on randomized compilation has not been thoroughly studied.
method: The authors simulate the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to generate ensembles of one-qubit rotations and compute the trace distance between the ideal quantum state and the state obtained after applying the discretized rotation from the SK decomposition.
result: The simulations show that the trace distance decreases as the SK approximation depth increases, and they characterize the trade-off between approximation accuracy and the number of gates used.
conclusion: The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm can effectively generate rotation ensembles for randomized compilation, but the overhead in gate count may limit practical applicability for near-term devices.

method: The authors use theoretical analysis and simulations to study droplet nucleation in active fluids with suppressed density fluctuations (hyperuniformity).
result: They find that the nucleation barrier is determined by a nonequilibrium quasipotential, and capillary-wave dynamics are modified by activity.

result: Successive freezing of spin and motional degrees of freedom observed; sensitivity achieved that constrains extraction of topological entropy.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a path to measure topological entropy in non-Abelian quantum phases, but the focus is on condensed matter physics rather than information thermodynamics.

motivation: Magic states are essential for universal quantum computing but costly to produce; efficient generation is needed.
method: Proposes tricycle codes, a family of QLDPC codes with high rate and constant-depth encoding, enabling magic state distillation.
result: Demonstrates that tricycle codes can generate CZ magic states with high fidelity and low overhead, outperforming existing schemes.
conclusion: Tricycle codes offer a practical path to efficient magic state generation, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

[PRX Quantum 7, 020350] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A moment-matching dilation framework maps nonunitary dynamics to a tight-binding lattice for near-optimal quantum simulation of linear differential equations.
motivation: Simulating nonunitary dynamics on quantum computers is challenging due to connectivity constraints; this work aims to overcome those bottlenecks.
method: The authors develop a dilation approach that uses a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice as an ancillary system, employing moment-matching to encode the nonunitary evolution into a unitary on the enlarged system.
result: The framework achieves near-optimal quantum algorithms for simulating linear differential equations, with improved resource scaling compared to previous methods.
conclusion: The proposed dilation technique provides an efficient and practical route for quantum simulation of nonunitary processes, relevant to quantum computing applications.

title: Fourier Neural Operators For Time-Periodic Quantum Systems: Learning Floquet Hamiltonians, Observable Dynamics, And Operator Growth
authors: Zihao Qi, Yang Peng, And Christopher Earls

motivation: Modeling periodically driven quantum systems is computationally expensive; neural operators offer a data-driven approach to capture temporal correlations.
method: Applies Fourier neural operators to learn the Floquet Hamiltonian and predict observable dynamics and operator growth from training data.
result: The method accurately extrapolates dynamics beyond the training time window and captures operator growth behavior.
conclusion: Fourier neural operators are effective for learning and predicting the behavior of time-periodic quantum systems.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols

tldr: The paper presents an efficient classical simulation method for logical magic state preparation protocols by propagating errors to the end of the circuit.
motivation: Magic state preparation is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating these protocols classically is often computationally expensive. The authors aim to make such simulations scalable and efficient.
method: They develop a technique that propagates errors through the circuit to the end, allowing the simulation to be performed with reduced overhead. This likely involves tracking Pauli errors and using stabilizer formalism.
result: The method achieves efficient classical simulation for a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols, demonstrating scalability.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for analyzing magic state preparation, which is important for resource estimation in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

authors: Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, And Leonid P. Pryadko
abstract:

motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction typically requires many rounds of syndrome extraction; single-shot error correction reduces this overhead.
method: The authors construct Abelian multi-cycle codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, and analyze their single-shot properties.

conclusion: These codes offer a practical advantage for fault-tolerant quantum computing by reducing the number of syndrome extraction rounds needed.

method: The authors introduce radial codes, a family of low-density parity-check codes with tunable parameters, and analyze their error correction capabilities using numerical simulations and theoretical bounds.
result: Radial codes achieve high thresholds, low overhead, and single-shot decoding, making them promising for near-term quantum devices.

result: The design achieves hardware-efficient universal linear transformations and exceeds performance thresholds for fault-tolerant quantum computation under realistic noise.
conclusion: Synthetic time dimensions offer a promising path to scalable photonic quantum computing by drastically reducing component count while maintaining full connectivity.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) for QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the expressiveness and trainability of variational quantum algorithms is crucial for their practical use; DLAs offer a theoretical tool to characterize barren plateaus.
method: The authors derive analytical bounds on DLA dimensions for general graphs and explicitly compute DLAs for cycle and complete graphs using Lie algebra decomposition.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and a semisimple component, and the variance of the cost function is computed, proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is determined.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA trainability, but the focus on combinatorial optimization and variational algorithms is not a core priority in the user's research interests.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of Clifford+Pauli quantum neural networks, showing they cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters with an average over four discrete Clifford values, enabling efficient classical simulation.
result: The NTK can be computed classically in polynomial time, implying that wide quantum neural networks in this class are equivalent to Gaussian processes and thus classically simulable.
conclusion: Such quantum neural networks cannot achieve quantum advantage, as their expected output can be computed classically.

title: Tensor Cross Interpolation Of Purities In Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Dmytro Kolisnyk, Raimel A. Medina, Romain Vasseur, And Maksym Serbyn
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2114 (2026).

A defining feature of quantum many-body systems is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with the number of degrees of freedom. This exponential complexity naïvely renders a complete state characterization, for instance via the complete set of bipartite Renyi entropies for all disjoint regions, a challenging task. Recently, a compact way of storing subregions' purities by encoding them as amplitudes of a fictitious quantum wave function, known as entanglement feature, was proposed. Notably, the entanglement feature can be a simple object even for highly entangled quantum states. However the complexity and practical usage of the entanglement feature for general quantum states has not been explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the entanglement feature can be efficiently learned using only a polynomial amount of samples in the number of degrees of freedom through the so-called tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm, assuming it is expressible as a finite bond dimension MPS. We benchmark this learning process on Haar and random MPS states, confirming analytic expectations. Applying the TCI algorithm to quantum eigenstates of various one dimensional quantum systems, we identify cases where eigenstates have entanglement feature learnable with TCI. We conclude with possible applications of the learned entanglement feature, such as quantifying the distance between different entanglement patterns and finding the optimal one-dimensional ordering of physical indices in a given state, highlighting the potential utility of the proposed purity interpolation method.

.
tldr: This paper uses tensor cross interpolation to efficiently learn the entanglement feature (set of bipartite purities) of quantum many-body states, demonstrating polynomial scaling for states with matrix product state structure.
motivation: Characterizing entanglement in many-body systems is exponentially hard; the entanglement feature offers a compact representation, but its practical extraction for general states was unexplored.
method: The authors apply the tensor cross interpolation (TCI) algorithm to learn the entanglement feature as a matrix product state from a polynomial number of samples, benchmarking on Haar random states and random MPS.
result: TCI can efficiently learn the entanglement feature for states that are expressible as finite bond-dimension MPS, including certain eigenstates of 1D quantum systems.
conclusion: The learned entanglement feature enables quantifying distances between entanglement patterns and finding optimal 1D orderings, suggesting practical utility for entanglement analysis.

title: Fully Optimised Variational Simulation Of A Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Lesley Gover, Vinul Wimalaweera, Fariha Azad, Matthew Decross, Michael Foss-Feig, And Andrew G. Green
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2109 (2026).

We time-evolve a translationally invariant quantum state on the Quantinuum H1-1 trapped-ion quantum processor, studying the dynamical quantum phase transition of the transverse field Ising model. This physics requires a delicate cancellation of phases in the many-body wavefunction and presents a tough challenge for current quantum devices. We follow the dynamics using a quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz, optimised for the time-evolution using a fidelity cost function. Sampling costs are mitigated by using the measured values of this circuit as stochastic corrections to a simple classical extrapolation of the ansatz parameters. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution and reveal a hitherto hidden simplicity of the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model through the dynamical quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: This paper uses a trapped-ion quantum processor to simulate a dynamical quantum phase transition in the transverse field Ising model using a variational quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz.
motivation: Dynamical quantum phase transitions are challenging to simulate on current quantum devices due to the need for delicate phase cancellations; the authors aim to demonstrate the feasibility of variational quantum time-evolution for such problems.
method: They implement a quantum circuit matrix product state ansatz optimized via a fidelity cost function, with stochastic corrections from measured circuit values to a classical extrapolation of ansatz parameters.
result: The variational approach successfully follows the dynamics and reveals a hidden simplicity in the evolution of the transverse-field Ising model through the dynamical quantum phase transition.
conclusion: The work shows that variational quantum time-evolution is a viable method for studying dynamical quantum phase transitions on current trapped-ion hardware.

title: Polynomial Time Constructive Decision Algorithm For Multivariable Quantum Signal Processing
authors: Yuki Ito, Hitomi Mori, Kazuki Sakamoto, And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2102 (2026).

Quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) have provided a unified framework for understanding many quantum algorithms, including factorization, matrix inversion, and Hamiltonian simulation. As a multivariable version of QSP, multivariable quantum signal processing (M-QSP) is proposed. M-QSP interleaves signal operators corresponding to each variable with signal processing operators, which provides an efficient means to perform multivariable polynomial transformations. However, the necessary and sufficient condition for what types of polynomials can be constructed by M-QSP is unknown. In this paper, we propose a classical algorithm to determine whether a given pair of multivariable Laurent polynomials can be implemented by M-QSP, which returns True or False. As one of the most important properties of this algorithm, its returning True is the necessary and sufficient condition. The proposed classical algorithm runs in polynomial time in the number of variables and signal operators. Our algorithm also provides a constructive method to select the necessary parameters for implementing M-QSP. These findings offer valuable insights for identifying practical applications of M-QSP.

.
tldr: A polynomial-time classical algorithm to decide whether a pair of multivariable Laurent polynomials can be implemented by M-QSP, providing necessary and sufficient conditions.
motivation: M-QSP generalizes QSP to multiple variables, but the exact class of implementable polynomials was unknown, limiting its application.
method: The authors develop a classical algorithm that checks feasibility by reducing to a system of polynomial equations solvable in polynomial time.
result: The algorithm runs in polynomial time in the number of variables and signal operators, and returns True iff the polynomial pair is implementable, also providing the required parameters.
conclusion: This work clarifies the expressibility of M-QSP and offers a constructive tool for designing quantum algorithms based on multivariable polynomial transformations.

title: A Quantum Kinetic Theory Of Photon Bose–Einstein Condensation In Semiconductors
authors: José L Figueiredo, Ross C Schofield, Ming Fu, Robert A Nyman, Rupert Oulton, Hugo Terças And Florian Mintert
abstract: Photon condensation in semiconductor microcavities is a transformative technique for engineering quantum states of light at room temperature by tailoring strong but incoherent light-matter interactions. While continuous-wave and electrical pumping offer exceptional prospects for miniaturized quantum photonic technologies, harnessing these requires conceptual advances in understanding non-equilibrium light-matter dynamics in semiconductors. We resolve this challenge through an ab initio quantum kinetic theory capturing how Coulomb interactions of optically excited carriers and phonon scattering mediate photon thermalization and condensation in semiconductors. Our microscopic model shows that at high carrier densities, thermalization is dominated by carrier–carrier Coulomb scattering, in clear contrast to the rovibrational relaxation that governs dye-based photon condensates. The theory predicts a rich nonequilibrium phase diagram with thermal, Bose-condensed, multimode, and lasing phases, quantitatively in agreement with recent experiments. Crucially, we identify how cavity detuning controls transitions between equilibrium and gain-dominated regimes, enabling tailored design of coherent light sources. This work thus provides the foundation for semiconductor-based quantum photonic devices operating beyond conventional laser paradigms.
tldr: A quantum kinetic theory of photon Bose-Einstein condensation in semiconductors, focusing on non-equilibrium light-matter dynamics.
motivation: To understand and control photon condensation in semiconductor microcavities for quantum photonic technologies.
method: Ab initio quantum kinetic theory incorporating Coulomb interactions and phonon scattering.
result: Predicts a non-equilibrium phase diagram with thermal, condensed, multimode, and lasing phases, validated by experiments.
conclusion: Provides a foundation for semiconductor-based quantum photonic devices beyond conventional lasers.

title: Amplitude-dependent Quantum Hydrodynamics From A \(\coth\)-Madelung Ansatz
authors: C. Dedes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a nonlinear extension of the Madelung transformation based on a hyperbolic phase--amplitude coupling of the form \[ \Psi = R e^{\imath\theta \coth R}, \] where \(R\) is a real amplitude field and \(\theta\) is an auxiliary phase coordinate governed by Schr\"odinger's equation. In contrast to the conventional polar decomposition, this construction imposes a singular hyperbolic relation between amplitude and phase, thereby endowing the Bohmian or hydrodynamic description with an intrinsically geometric structure. We show that the associated velocity field acquires a density-gradient contribution, producing generalized continuity equations and modified quantum force terms. When interpreted as a complex macroscopic order parameter, this generalized phase structure leads to modified superconducting electrodynamics; in particular, the London equations acquire additional contributions that render the Meissner response sensitive to spatial density gradients. The proposed framework is motivated by broader developments involving complex group velocities, dissipative wave propagation, and amplitude-sensitive transport in quantum systems.
tldr: A nonlinear Madelung transformation with hyperbolic phase-amplitude coupling leads to modified quantum hydrodynamics and superconducting electrodynamics.
motivation: To explore a geometric extension of the Madelung transformation that introduces amplitude-dependent phase contributions, potentially revealing new hydrodynamic and superconducting phenomena.
method: The paper proposes a coth-Madelung ansatz Ψ = R e^{iθ coth R}, derives generalized continuity equations and quantum force terms, and applies the formalism to superconducting electrodynamics.
result: The velocity field acquires density-gradient contributions, and the London equations gain additional terms making the Meissner response sensitive to spatial density gradients.
conclusion: The framework provides a novel geometric structure to quantum hydrodynamics and suggests amplitude-sensitive transport effects, but remains theoretical without direct experimental or information-theoretic implications.

title: Quantum Correlations And Coherence In A Two-qubit Anisotropic $xy$ Under Magnetic Field
authors: Ahmed Jellal, Pablo D\'iaz, David Laroze
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study thermal quantum correlations and coherence in Heisenberg [MATH] model with anisotropic interactions under a uniform magnetic field [MATH]. Using concurrence [MATH], local quantum uncertainty (LQU), Bell-Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) nonlocality [MATH], and coherence [MATH] as quantifiers, we analyze how magnetic anisotropy [MATH], coupling anisotropy [MATH], Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction [MATH], temperature [MATH], and magnetic field [MATH] modulate quantum resources. At low temperatures and relevant magnetic fields, the entanglement is maximized, but exhibits sudden death for [MATH], which turns into a smooth decay as [MATH] increases, highlighting its stabilizing role. LQU shows that stronger anisotropy suppresses quantum correlations, while [MATH] induces a non-monotonic response peaking at a critical field [MATH]. Bell-CHSH nonlocality violations ([MATH]) persist below [MATH], but thermal noise ([MATH]) suppresses them. Coherence [MATH] is most robust to thermal fluctuations, especially for high \( \delta_m \), which also dampens abrupt quantum phase transitions. The DM interaction is essential for entanglement generation, with [MATH] and anisotropy synergistically enhancing correlation resilience. We identify a hierarchy of thermal degradation: nonlocality ([MATH]) vanishes first, followed by entanglement ([MATH]), then general quantum correlations (LQU), while coherence [MATH] persists the longest. These results demonstrate tunable control of quantum resources via anisotropy and external parameters, providing insights for the design of robust spin-based quantum technologies.

result: Demonstrates significant enhancement of photon drag due to slow-light effects and tunneling coupling.

title: Robust Applicability Of Continuous Dynamical Decoupling To Decoherence Reduction In Longitudinal And Transverse-noise Settings: The Role Of Anisotropy
authors: S. Afonso, J. M. Gomez Llorente, And J. Plata

We analytically evaluate the efficiency of continuous dynamical decoupling (CDD) to curb decoherence in generic qubit setups where diverse sources of noise can be present. Previous theoretical approaches to CDD have mainly focused on its potential to cope with longitudinal fluctuations. Here, the ba…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062412] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Analytical evaluation of continuous dynamical decoupling for decoherence reduction in qubit setups with both longitudinal and transverse noise, highlighting the role of noise anisotropy.
motivation: Previous CDD studies focused on longitudinal noise; this work extends to transverse noise and anisotropic settings to assess robustness.
method: Analytical derivation of decoherence suppression efficiency using CDD for generic qubit noise models with arbitrary anisotropy.
result: CDD effectively reduces decoherence in both longitudinal and transverse noise, but its efficiency depends on noise anisotropy and control parameters.
conclusion: CDD is a robust technique for decoherence mitigation in diverse noise environments, with practical implications for quantum memory and gates.

tldr: This paper studies localization and scattering of a single photon in waveguide-coupled qubit arrays with quasiperiodic spacings, revealing a continuum of long-lived subradiant states.
motivation: Understanding photon transport in disordered quantum systems is important for quantum networks and light-matter interfaces.
method: The authors model a waveguide coupled to qubit arrays with quasiperiodic spacings and analyze the scattering properties and localization of single photons using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They find that as quasiperiodic strength increases, localized subradiant states with extremely long lifetimes form a continuum band around the resonant frequency, contrasting with the discrete bound states in periodic arrays.
conclusion: Quasiperiodic qubit arrays can host a continuum of long-lived subradiant states, which may be useful for quantum memory or slow-light applications.

The experimental detection of nonequilibrium quantum criticality remains a challenge, as traditional signatures like dynamical quantum phase transitions rely on hard-to-measure global properties. Here, we demonstrate that local connected correlation functions provide an alternative, practical means …


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062204] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses local connected correlation functions to probe the crossover between dynamical phases in a Rydberg-atom array, offering a practical alternative to global order parameters.
motivation: Detecting nonequilibrium quantum criticality is challenging because traditional signatures like dynamical quantum phase transitions rely on hard-to-measure global properties.
method: The authors numerically simulate a Rydberg-atom array and compute local connected correlation functions to identify dynamical phase transitions.
result: Local correlations can effectively signal the crossover between different dynamical phases, providing a measurable proxy for global order parameters.
conclusion: Local correlation functions are a practical tool for detecting nonequilibrium criticality in experimental quantum simulators.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Devices Beyond Classical Capabilities

Rapid development of quantum computing technology has led to a wide variety of sophisticated quantum devices. Benchmarking these systems becomes crucial for understanding their capabilities and paving the way for future advancements. The Quantum Volume (QV) test is one of the most widely used benchm…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062604] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a benchmarking method for quantum devices using the Quantum Volume test and related metrics, focusing on assessing computational capability beyond classical simulation.
motivation: As quantum devices grow in complexity, reliable benchmarking is essential to understand their capabilities and guide development. The Quantum Volume test is widely used but may not capture all aspects of device performance.
method: The authors analyze the Quantum Volume test and propose modifications or alternative metrics to better benchmark quantum devices, possibly using random circuit sampling or other complexity measures.
result: The paper likely presents a new benchmarking protocol or analysis that improves upon existing methods, providing a more comprehensive assessment of quantum device performance.
conclusion: Benchmarking methods like Quantum Volume are useful but need refinement to accurately reflect device capabilities beyond classical simulation, and the proposed approach offers a step forward.

title: Strange Metal Behavior In A Toy Model With Selective Mottness
authors: M. S. Laad And S. R. Hassan

Author(s): M. S. Laad and S. R. Hassan

The interplay between band and atomic aspects in materials with coexisting wide-band and flat-band states, or wide-band and effectively dispersionless electronic states is increasingly expected to lead to novel behavior. Using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), we investigate strange metal-like beh…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235111] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: A DMFT study of strange metal behavior in a toy model with selective Mottness, focusing on non-Fermi liquid transport.
motivation: To understand the interplay between band and atomic aspects in materials with coexisting wide-band and flat-band states, which may lead to novel strange metal behavior.
method: Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) is used to investigate the electronic properties of a toy model exhibiting selective Mottness.
result: The model reproduces strange metal-like behavior, including linear-in-temperature resistivity and other non-Fermi liquid signatures.
conclusion: Selective Mottness provides a mechanism for strange metal behavior, relevant to understanding high-temperature superconductors and other correlated materials.

title: Cellular Automata In $d$ Dimensions And Ground States Of Spin Models In $(d+1)$ Dimensions
authors: Konstantinos Sfairopoulos, Luke Causer, Jamie F. Mair, And Juan P. Garrahan

We show how the trajectories of [MATH]-dimensional cellular automata (CA) can be used to systematically construct the ground states of [MATH]-dimensional classical spin models, and we characterize their quantum phase transition, when in the presence of a transverse magnetic field. For each of the 256 …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064112] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper constructs ground states of (d+1)-dimensional classical spin models from d-dimensional cellular automata trajectories and studies their quantum phase transitions.
motivation: To establish a systematic connection between cellular automata and classical spin models, enabling the study of quantum phase transitions in the resulting spin systems.
method: The authors map trajectories of d-dimensional cellular automata to ground states of (d+1)-dimensional classical spin models, then add a transverse field to study quantum phase transitions.
result: They characterize the quantum phase transitions for all 256 elementary cellular automata rules, showing that the critical behavior is determined by the CA rule.
conclusion: Cellular automata provide a useful tool for constructing and analyzing classical spin models and their quantum phase transitions, but the work is primarily a mathematical mapping without direct thermodynamic or information-theoretic implications.

We examined the Brownian motion of point defects in a two-dimensional hexagonal colloidal crystal, going beyond the conventional treatment that assumes constant diffusion coefficients. By extracting the spatially varying drift vector and diffusion matrix directly from experimental trajectories, we u…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065404] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Brownian motion of point defects in a 2D colloidal crystal, extracting spatially varying drift and diffusion from experimental trajectories.
motivation: To go beyond constant diffusion coefficient models and understand defect dynamics in periodic potentials.
method: Experimental trajectories of point defects in a hexagonal colloidal lattice are analyzed to extract spatially varying drift vector and diffusion matrix.
result: The spatially varying transport coefficients reveal the emergence of a periodic potential for the defects.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed characterization of defect motion in a colloidal crystal, but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Violation Of Local Equilibrium Thermodynamics In One-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts Model

The fractional derivative is introduced so as to reproduce the low-wave-number density of states of th…

motivation: To understand nonequilibrium phase transitions and test the validity of local equilibrium assumptions in systems with long-range interactions.
method: Numerical simulation of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian-Potts model with fractional spatial derivatives to reproduce low-wave-number density of states.
result: The system exhibits violation of local equilibrium thermodynamics during phase coexistence.
conclusion: Fractional derivatives lead to nonlocal effects that break local equilibrium, highlighting limitations of standard thermodynamic descriptions.

conclusion: The work provides illustrative examples of dynamical phase transitions in nonergodic stochastic processes, contributing to the theory of non-equilibrium systems.

The linearized limit of this model val…

tldr: This paper studies heat conduction in a 1D chain of rotors with nonlinear interactions, revealing a transition from ballistic to diffusive transport due to nonlinearity.
motivation: Understanding heat transport in low-dimensional systems is fundamental for nanoscale thermal management and reveals effects of topology and nonlinearity.
method: The authors model a chain of coupled rotors with a topological linear limit and introduce nonlinear couplings, then compute heat current via molecular dynamics simulations and analytical approximations.
result: Nonlinearity induces a transition from ballistic to diffusive heat conduction, with the thermal conductivity scaling with system size in a nontrivial way.
conclusion: Nonlinearity can destroy topological protection of ballistic transport, leading to normal heat conduction in a system that is ballistic in the linear regime.

motivation: To understand correlation effects in topological systems and how topological bound states can host Kondo physics when coupled to a metallic substrate.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on nonlinear optical control and metastable phases.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems, which may lead to novel material properties and quantum phases.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, including time-resolved spectroscopy and dynamical mean-field theory simulations.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable states, and transient orders (superconducting, magnetic, etc.) in Mott insulators.
conclusion: Photoexcitation provides a powerful tool to engineer nonequilibrium states, but the field is still developing and many open questions remain.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium reviewing materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations as due to violated assumptions in measurement.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many materials exhibit properties that seem to exceed these bounds, prompting a need to understand the underlying assumptions and how they can be circumvented.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of materials and measurements where such violations occur, categorizing them by which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated.
result: It identifies that apparent violations arise because measurements are made in ways that violate assumptions such as equilibrium, homogeneity, or linearity, and shows how designed materials can exploit these violations.
conclusion: The findings clarify that thermodynamic bounds are not violated in a fundamental sense, but rather that careful consideration of assumptions is needed; this opens avenues for engineering materials with extreme properties.

title: Construction And Decoding Of Quantum Margulis Codes
authors: Michele Pacenti, Dimitris Chytas, And Bane Vasić
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2101 (2026).

Quantum low-density parity-check codes are a promising approach to fault-tolerant quantum computation, offering potential advantages in rate and decoding efficiency. In this work, we introduce quantum Margulis codes, a new class of QLDPC codes derived from Margulis' classical LDPC construction via the two-block group algebra framework. We show that quantum Margulis codes, unlike bivariate bicycle codes which require ordered statistics decoding for effective error correction, can be efficiently decoded using a standard min-sum decoder with linear complexity, when decoded under the code capacity noise model. This is attributed to their Tanner graph structure, which does not exhibit group symmetry, thereby mitigating the well-known problem of error degeneracy in QLDPC decoding. To further enhance performance, we propose an algorithm for constructing 2BGA codes with controlled girth, ensuring a minimum girth of 6 or 8, and use it to generate several quantum Margulis codes of length 240 and 642. We validate our approach through numerical simulations, demonstrating that quantum Margulis codes behave significantly better than BB codes in the error floor region, under min-sum decoding.

.
tldr: Introduces quantum Margulis codes, a new class of QLDPC codes with efficient min-sum decoding and improved error floor performance.
motivation: To construct QLDPC codes that can be decoded with linear complexity while avoiding error degeneracy, which plagues bivariate bicycle codes.
method: Derives codes from Margulis' classical LDPC construction via the two-block group algebra framework and proposes an algorithm to control girth.
result: Quantum Margulis codes of length 240 and 642 achieve better error floor performance than BB codes under min-sum decoding.
conclusion: Quantum Margulis codes are a promising alternative for fault-tolerant quantum computation due to their efficient decoding and good performance.

title: Geometry-resolved Suppression Of Patch-potential Heating In Skeleton-electrode Ion Traps
authors: Chon-Teng Belmiro Chu, Hao-Chung Chen, Ting Hsu, Hsiang-Yu Lo, Ming-Shien Chang And Guin-Dar Lin
abstract: We present a quantitative, geometry-resolved framework to evaluate the effects of patch-potential noise in realistic three-dimensional Paul-trap structures. As a concrete application, we analyze a skeleton-electrode architecture and compare its performance against a conventional blade trap under identical ion-to-electrode distances and matched confinement parameters. The skeleton geometry achieves a suppression of motional heating exceeding 50%, with heating rate ratios of for the axial mode and for the radial mode. Patch-by-patch heating maps reveal that over 99% of the noise contribution originates from electrode surfaces within 500 m of the ion. We identify that axial heating follows a non-monotonic profile, with dominant ‘hotspots’ located at an intermediate distance of approximately 110 m. This behavior is driven by the vectorial directionality of the electric-field components, which provide the strongest axial coupling at these intermediate regions. Guided by these maps, we demonstrate a proof-of-principle electrode reconfiguration where segmented gaps are aligned with identified hotspots. This strategy successfully reduces axial heating even when the total electrode surface area increases, confirming that the spatial distribution of noise coupling—rather than total conductor area—is the primary driver of motional heating. These findings establish geometry-guided design as a practical route to suppress heating in trapped-ion platform, and the proposed skeleton architecture is compatible with advanced fabrication techniques, including metal additive manufacturing.
tldr: A geometry-resolved framework to suppress patch-potential heating in ion traps by analyzing noise contributions and reconfiguring electrode gaps.
motivation: Motional heating from patch potentials limits trapped-ion quantum computing performance; understanding its spatial origin can guide trap design.
method: Quantitative modeling of patch-potential noise in 3D Paul traps, comparing skeleton-electrode and blade trap geometries, with patch-by-patch heating maps.
result: Skeleton geometry suppresses heating by >50%; axial heating hotspots identified at ~110 μm; electrode reconfiguration reduces heating even with increased surface area.
conclusion: Spatial distribution of noise coupling, not total conductor area, dominates heating; geometry-guided design offers a practical route to suppress heating in ion traps.

title: Fate Of The Ising Universality Class Under Nonreciprocal Interactions
authors: M. Akritidis, A. Garc\'es, A. Vasilopoulos, M. Carosi, D. Levis, N. G. Fytas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the critical behavior of a two-dimensional Ising model with nonreciprocal vision-cone interactions, which explicitly violate reciprocity and detailed balance. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and dynamic renormalization-group analysis show that the asymptotic critical exponents remain fully consistent with the equilibrium Ising universality class over a broad range of nonreciprocal coupling strengths [MATH]. In contrast, dimensionless quantities such as the Binder cumulant and the correlation-length ratio display pronounced anisotropic nonequilibrium corrections and systematically deviate from their equilibrium Ising values. The renormalization-group flow further demonstrates that the nonreciprocal perturbation is irrelevant at the Wilson-Fisher fixed point while generating a finite shift of the critical temperature proportional to [MATH]. Our results demonstrate the remarkable robustness of two-dimensional Ising criticality against this class of directional interactions.
tldr: The 2D Ising model with nonreciprocal interactions retains equilibrium Ising critical exponents but shows anisotropic nonequilibrium corrections.
motivation: To understand how nonreciprocal interactions, which break detailed balance, affect the universality class of the 2D Ising model.
method: Combined Monte Carlo simulations and dynamic renormalization-group analysis.
result: Critical exponents remain unchanged, but dimensionless quantities like Binder cumulant deviate from equilibrium values; the nonreciprocal perturbation is irrelevant at the Wilson-Fisher fixed point.
conclusion: 2D Ising criticality is robust against nonreciprocal vision-cone interactions, with only finite-temperature shifts and anisotropic corrections.

title: Breakdown Of The Thermodynamic Limit In Quantum Spin And Dimer Models

title: Information Theoretic Measures Of Isotropic Dunkl Oscillator In Spherical Coordinates
authors: Akash Halder, Amlan K. Roy, Debraj Nath
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An information theoretic analysis is done for the isotropic harmonic oscillator potential within the Dunkl-Schr\"odinger framework in spherical coordinates. Starting from the exact analytical eigensolution, various quantum information measures such as Shannon entropy, R\'enyi information, Tsallis entropy are derived. Besides, their relative measures like relative Shannon, relative R\'enyi, relative Tsallis as well as corresponding divergences (Jensen-Shannon, Jensen-R\'enyi, Jensen-Tsallis) are also obtained. In order to get Shannon entropy, a novel factorization method is introduced. This is facilitated through the use of well-known weighted Lebesgue measure. The results from the Dunkl case agree exactly with the non-Dunkl scenario, when Dunkl parameters vanish. The reflection operators and Dunkl parameters considerably influence the above measures. These are portrayed in graphical forms.
tldr: This paper computes information-theoretic measures for the isotropic Dunkl oscillator, a deformed quantum system, in spherical coordinates.
motivation: To extend quantum information measures to non-standard quantum systems with reflection operators and Dunkl parameters.
method: Exact analytical solutions of the Dunkl-Schrödinger equation are used to derive Shannon, Rényi, and Tsallis entropies and their relative measures via a novel factorization method.
result: Analytical expressions for various entropy measures are obtained, showing dependence on Dunkl parameters and reducing to standard oscillator results when parameters vanish.
conclusion: The Dunkl oscillator provides a testbed for studying information measures in deformed quantum systems, but the work is primarily mathematical and lacks direct connection to core quantum information topics.

result: They find a first-order liquid-gas phase transition and a critical point, with the droplet phase stabilized by exchange correlations.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical description of thermal effects on dipolar Fermi droplets, but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics of computation.

title: Imaginary Time Spectral Transforms For Excited-state Preparation
