tldr: A variational method for preparing excited eigenstates of many-body quantum systems using imaginary time spectral transforms and tensor networks.
motivation: Preparing excited states is important for understanding quantum systems, but existing methods are often computationally expensive or require matrix inversion.
method: Combines a shift-invert spectral transformation with imaginary time evolution to avoid explicit matrix inversion, implemented via tensor-network simulations.
result: Demonstrated on disordered spin chains, showing accurate preparation of excited eigenstates.
conclusion: The method provides a viable approach for excited-state preparation compatible with hybrid quantum-classical implementations.

title: Cyclic Ladder Operators And Hidden Weyl-Heisenberg Structure In A Floquet System
authors: Li Ge Tianao Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ladder operators, found in the quantum harmonic oscillator and other quantized systems, provide an elegant approach to solving or understanding otherwise intricate physics problems. In this Letter, we discuss cyclic ladder operators in both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems with a finite Hilbert space, with the highest (lowest) level directly descending (ascending) to the lowest (highest) level via a single raising (lowering) operation. We show that an equally spaced energy ladder emerges when these systems have an underlying Weyl-Heisenberg commutation relation, with the cyclic ladder operators and the temporal evolution operator behaving as the generators of the Weyl-Heisenberg group. We further illustrate such a system using a one-dimensional Floquet lattice, where the cyclic ladder operators become diagonal and the temporal evolution simplifies to a permutation matrix after a Floquet period. Our findings reveal a hidden relation between non-trivial dynamics and algebraic principles in Floquet systems, which may exist for other quantum numbers as well besides the energy levels.
tldr: The paper introduces cyclic ladder operators in finite Hilbert spaces and reveals a hidden Weyl-Heisenberg structure in a Floquet system.
motivation: To generalize ladder operators to cyclic systems and uncover algebraic structures underlying Floquet dynamics.
method: The authors define cyclic ladder operators for Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems with finite Hilbert space, show that equally spaced energy ladders arise from Weyl-Heisenberg commutation relations, and illustrate with a 1D Floquet lattice.
result: Cyclic ladder operators and the temporal evolution operator generate the Weyl-Heisenberg group; in the Floquet lattice, the evolution becomes a permutation matrix after one period.
conclusion: The findings reveal a hidden relation between non-trivial dynamics and algebraic principles in Floquet systems, potentially applicable to other quantum numbers.

title: Complex-gauge Control Of Anomalous Floquet Corner Responses In A non-Hermitian Physical-synthetic Photonic Lattice
authors: X. Z. Zhang W. C. Ning
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a non-Hermitian Floquet photonic lattice formed by a physical resonator coordinate and a synthetic frequency coordinate. A two-step modulation protocol realizes a chiral walk in this physical-synthetic plane, with a real synthetic flux controlling loop interference and imaginary gauge fields controlling non-reciprocal envelopes. We show that anomalous corner pairs at quasienergies zero and \(\pi/T\) exhibit three distinct layers of physics. A non-Bloch higher-order construction predicts whether the \(0/\pi\) corner pair exists under open boundaries. The imaginary gauge fields select where the right eigenmodes accumulate. The real flux controls the local interference matrix element that determines whether the doubled-period optical response is visible. As a result, the same topological coexistence sector can be bright, skin-dark, or flux-dark in a local optical measurement. We further show that the complex gauge can tune an exceptional point of the two-period corner propagator. At this point the anomalous response keeps its doubled-period sign alternation, but its envelope becomes algebraic because of a Jordan block. These results provide a photonic route to separate topological existence, skin-selected localization, optical visibility, and defective two-period dynamics in a non-Hermitian synthetic dimension.
tldr: A non-Hermitian Floquet photonic lattice with synthetic dimensions exhibits anomalous corner responses controlled by complex gauge fields.
motivation: To explore topological phenomena in non-Hermitian systems with synthetic dimensions and demonstrate control over corner states via complex gauge fields.
method: The authors construct a non-Hermitian Floquet photonic lattice using a physical resonator and a synthetic frequency coordinate, with a two-step modulation protocol implementing a chiral walk. They analyze the system using non-Bloch theory and study the effects of real and imaginary gauge fields on corner modes.
result: They find that anomalous corner pairs at quasienergies zero and π/T exhibit three layers of physics: existence, skin-selected localization, and optical visibility. An exceptional point in the corner propagator leads to algebraic envelope decay.
conclusion: The work provides a photonic platform to separate topological existence, localization, visibility, and dynamics in non-Hermitian synthetic dimensions, but does not directly connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Xiangnan Li, Tao Jiang, Chenrong Xia, Guoguo Xin, And Wenjing Zhang

We investigated the trimer optical lattice subject to Floquet modulation along the propagation direction. tldr: This paper studies Floquet-induced topological edge states in a trimer optical lattice, focusing on adiabatic transitions between Floquet and Bloch modes.
motivation: To understand how Floquet modulation can create localized edge states and how these states transition between Floquet and Bloch topological regimes.
method: Numerical calculations and finite element simulations of a trimer optical lattice with Floquet modulation along the propagation direction, combined with quasienergy band analysis.

title: Entanglement-enhanced Correlation Propagation In The One-dimensional $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ Fermi-Hubbard Model
authors: Mathias Mikkelsen And Ippei Danshita

[Phys. Rev. A 113, L061301] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies entanglement-enhanced correlation propagation in SU(N) Fermi-Hubbard models, showing that entangled initial states can increase propagation velocity up to the Bose-Hubbard limit.
motivation: Understanding how entanglement affects correlation spreading in many-body systems is important for quantum dynamics and transport.
method: The authors use an analytic model of excitations and numerical simulations for N=2,3,4,6 to compute correlation propagation velocities.
result: Entangled initial states enhance correlation propagation velocity, bounded by the Bose-Hubbard model velocity, which is reached in the large N limit.

title: Spin-triplet Pairing And Spin Supercurrent In $p$-wave Magnetic Superconductors
authors: Xing-Jian Yi, Yue Mao, Peng-Yi Liu, Yu-Fei Sun, And Qing-Feng Sun

motivation: To explore spin-triplet superconductivity in p-wave magnetic materials as a platform for dissipationless spin transport.
method: Theoretical analysis using mean-field theory and Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations to model the superconducting state and spin transport.
result: Predicts spin-triplet pairing and spin supercurrent in p-wave magnetic superconductors.

method: The authors use theoretical modeling and band structure calculations to analyze the effect of material parameters on the topology of moiré flat bands.
result: They identify conditions for topological phase transitions and characterize the resulting Chern insulator phases.
conclusion: The work provides insights into tuning topological properties in twisted bilayer graphene/hBN heterostructures.

result: They show that the decay of flat-band projectors is controlled by the algebraic properties of the CLS set, with singular sets leading to slower decay.
conclusion: The work provides a classification of flat bands based on CLS properties, but has no direct application to the user's research interests.

title: Randomly Twisted Bilayer Graphene: Cascade Transitions
authors: Baruch Horovitz And Pierre Le Doussal
abstract:

Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) is known to have disorder in its twist angle. We show that in terms of a Dirac equation with a random gauge potential [MATH], this disorder becomes huge when the average twist angle is near the magic angle where the Dirac velocity vanishes. The densit…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235113] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies disorder effects in twisted bilayer graphene near the magic angle, modeling it as a Dirac equation with random gauge potential and analyzing cascade transitions.
motivation: Twisted bilayer graphene exhibits strong correlations and superconductivity near the magic angle, but disorder in the twist angle can significantly affect its properties. Understanding these disorder effects is crucial for interpreting experiments.
method: The authors model the system using a Dirac equation with a random gauge potential, which becomes large near the magic angle due to vanishing Dirac velocity. They analyze the density of states and transport properties using field-theoretic methods.

conclusion: Disorder in the twist angle is a key factor in twisted bilayer graphene, and its effects must be accounted for to understand the experimental phase diagram.

title: Accurate Computation Of The Energy Variance For Ground States And $〈〈{\mathcal{L}}^{†}\mathcal{L}〉〉$ For Steady States Using iPEPS

method: The authors develop an approach to compute the energy variance of an iPEPS and extend it to compute the variance of the Lindbladian for steady states of open quantum systems.
result: The method is demonstrated on the 2D Heisenberg model and a dissipative transverse-field Ising model, showing improved accuracy over previous techniques.

result: The method provides an alternative to infinite DMRG for finite-size calculations that faithfully reproduce thermodynamic limit properties.

motivation: To explore level repulsion beyond Dyson's threefold way, specifically quartic repulsion without symplectic symmetry, which is rarely observed.
method: The authors study a three-body quantum system and analyze its energy level statistics using random matrix theory and numerical diagonalization.
result: They observe quartic level repulsion, which is stronger than the quadratic repulsion typical of the orthogonal class, and attribute it to the system's three-body interactions.
conclusion: The finding extends the understanding of quantum chaos and level statistics beyond conventional symmetry classes.

method: Proposes Quantum Feature-Map Learning via Analytic Iterative Reconstructions (Q-FL…) to iteratively construct feature maps with reduced gate count and depth.

title: Distinct Reentrant Transitions In A Quasiperiodic Raman Lattice

motivation: To explore reentrant phenomena in quasiperiodic systems beyond the usual extended-localized transitions, including critical phases.
method: The authors analyze a one-dimensional Raman lattice model with spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman potential containing both uniform and quasiperiodic components, using numerical methods to identify phase boundaries.
result: They find multiple reentrant transitions into a critical phase, extending the known reentrant behavior to include critical states.
conclusion: The work reveals richer phase diagrams in quasiperiodic systems, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Pathway To Kondo Physics In Quantum Wires Coupled To A Repulsive Spin Impurity And Manifestations In Ytterbium Atoms

method: The authors use theoretical and numerical methods to analyze the Kondo singlet formation in quantum wires with a repulsive spin impurity.
result: They find that the Kondo effect persists even with repulsive interactions, and predict observable signatures in ytterbium atom experiments.
conclusion: The work extends Kondo physics to repulsive impurities in one dimension, offering new insights into strongly correlated systems.

conclusion: The architecture is a powerful tool for quantum many-body problems, but the paper focuses on computational methods rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Evolving Disorder In non-Hermitian Lattices

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; this review aims to provide a pedagogical overview of space-time duality as a unifying framework.
method: The paper reviews the concept of space-time duality in lattice systems, focusing on brickwork quantum circuits and their relationship to exactly solvable dynamics.
result: It presents a unified view of dynamical evolution in quantum many-body systems through the lens of quantum computation and circuit models.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful tool for understanding and solving quantum many-body dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium reviewing synthetic quantum matter in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions, focusing on simulation of condensed matter and gravity phenomena.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries that are difficult to realize naturally, enabling simulation of topological and gravitational models.
method: Reviews experimental implementations in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems, including lattice engineering and synthetic dimensions.
result: Summarizes progress in realizing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher-dimensional physics in synthetic quantum systems.
conclusion: These platforms offer new avenues for studying exotic quantum phenomena, but the paper is a broad review without deep technical contributions to the user's specific directions.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and a generalized index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a symmetry, which is a topic in quantum computation theory.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define invariants (anyon permutation and GNVW-like index) and shows equivalence to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification for subalgebra QCAs on regular representations of finite Abelian groups, with an example of Kramers-Wannier duality.
conclusion: Subalgebra QCAs are classified by two invariants, and the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement in atom interferometers using spin-squeezed states under realistic loss conditions.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but losses degrade performance.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses, and one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but finite temperature poses challenges.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: The paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to lithium atom's quartet state.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying Pauli principle and variable bosonic excitations.
result: A benchmark wave function of lithium's quartet state is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Hidden Time-nonlocal Floquet Symmetries
authors: Sigmund Kohler And Jesús Casado-Pascual
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2112 (2026).

We investigate the Floquet spectrum of a detuned, driven two-level system and show that it exhibits exact quasienergy crossings when the detuning is an integer multiple of the energy quantum of the driving field. This behavior can be explained by a hidden time-nonlocal parity, which allows the Floquet modes to be classified as even or odd. Then a generic feature is the emergence of exact crossings between quasienergies of different parity. A constructive proof of the existence of the symmetry is based on a scalar recurrence relation. Moreover, we present a general scheme for its numerical computation, which can be applied to models beyond the two-level system. Analytical results are illustrated with numerical data.

.
tldr: The paper studies hidden time-nonlocal symmetries in driven two-level systems, leading to exact quasienergy crossings.
motivation: Understanding spectral properties of driven quantum systems is important for Floquet engineering, but the paper focuses on symmetry classification rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of the Floquet spectrum using a scalar recurrence relation to prove the existence of a hidden parity symmetry.
result: Exact quasienergy crossings occur when detuning is an integer multiple of the driving frequency, classified by a hidden time-nonlocal parity.
conclusion: The hidden symmetry explains level crossings and can be generalized to other driven systems.

title: Learning Symmetry-protected Topological Order From Trapped-ion Experiments
authors: Nicolas Sadoune, Ivan Pogorelov, Claire L. Edmunds, Giuliano Giudici, Giacomo Giudice, Christian D. Marciniak, Martin Ringbauer, Thomas Monz, And Lode Pollet
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2100 (2026).

Classical machine learning has proven remarkably useful in post-processing quantum data, yet typical learning algorithms often require prior training to be effective. In this work, we employ a tensorial kernel support vector machine (TK-SVM) to analyze experimental data produced by trapped-ion quantum computers. This unsupervised method benefits from directly interpretable training parameters, allowing it to identify the non-trivial string-order characterizing symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases. We apply our technique to two examples: a spin-1/2 model and a spin-1 model, featuring the cluster state and the AKLT state as paradigmatic instances of SPT order, respectively. Using matrix product states, we generate a family of quantum circuits that host a trivial phase and an SPT phase, with a sharp phase transition between them. For the spin-1 case, we implement these circuits on two distinct trapped-ion machines based on qubits and qutrits. Our results demonstrate that the TK-SVM method successfully distinguishes the two phases across all noisy experimental datasets, highlighting its robustness and effectiveness in quantum data interpretation.

.
tldr: Uses a tensorial kernel support vector machine to identify symmetry-protected topological order from trapped-ion experimental data.
motivation: Classical machine learning can help interpret quantum data, but typical methods require prior training; an unsupervised interpretable method is desirable.
method: Applies a tensorial kernel support vector machine (TK-SVM) to experimental data from trapped-ion quantum computers, using matrix product states to generate circuits hosting trivial and SPT phases.
result: The TK-SVM successfully distinguishes trivial and SPT phases across noisy experimental datasets from qubit and qutrit trapped-ion machines.
conclusion: The method is robust and effective for identifying SPT order in experimental quantum data without prior training.

title: Optimizing Qubo On A Quantum Computer By Mimicking Imaginary Time Evolution
authors: Yahui Chai And Alice Di Tucci
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems using an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC). The circuit parameters are optimized to mimic short-time ITE, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values. This significantly reduces the measurement overhead by avoiding full energy evaluation. By updating the initial state based on results from last step iteratively, the algorithm quickly converges to the low-energy solutions. With a pre-sorting step that optimizes quantum gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients, the convergence is further improved. Our classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above up to 150 qubits. Furthermore, the linear scaling of entanglement entropy with system size suggests that the circuit is challenging to simulate classically using tensor networks. We also demonstrate hardware runs on IBM’s device for 40, 60, and 80 qubits, and obtain solutions compatible with that from simulated annealing.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving QUBO problems using a circuit that mimics imaginary time evolution, with classical simulations up to 150 qubits and hardware runs on IBM devices.
motivation: QUBO problems are important for combinatorial optimization, but current quantum algorithms face measurement overhead and convergence issues. The authors aim to reduce measurement cost and improve convergence.
method: The algorithm uses an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC) optimized with single- and two-qubit expectation values, iterative state updates, and a pre-sorting step for gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients.
result: Classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above 0.9 for up to 150 qubits, and hardware runs on IBM devices for 40, 60, and 80 qubits yield solutions compatible with simulated annealing.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm efficiently solves QUBO problems on near-term quantum devices with reduced measurement overhead and good convergence, though it is not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Integrated Error-suppressed Pipeline For Quantum Optimization Of Nontrivial Binary Combinatorial Optimization Problems On Gate-model Hardware At The 156-qubit Scale
authors: Natasha Sachdeva, Gavin S Hartnett, Smarak Maity, Samuel Marsh, Yulun Wang, Adam Winick, Ryan Dougherty, Daniel Canuto, You Quan Chong, G Adam Cox, Michael Hush, Pranav S Mundada, Christopher D B Bentley, Michael J Biercuk And Yuval Baum
abstract: We introduce a novel hybrid quantum–classical variational optimization method for unconstrained binary combinatorial optimization problems on gate-model quantum computers, integrating a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based dual variational parameter update strategies, efficient parametric compilation, automated error suppression during hardware execution, and scalable O( ) classical post-processing to correct for bitflip errors. Without this integrated approach, we show that standard circuit execution at scale produces output indistinguishable from random sampling, establishing the necessity of each pipeline component. We benchmark the method on IBM superconducting quantum computers for several optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes, where the optimization is conducted on hardware with no use of classical simulation or prior knowledge of the solution. For Max-Cut on random regular graphs with topologies not matched to device connectivity, the method achieves approximation ratios (AR) of 100% for unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes, weighted regular graphs up to 80 nodes, and weighted 7-regular graphs up 50 nodes. Applied to higher-order binary optimization, the method finds the ground state energy of 127- and 156-qubit spin-glass models matched to device topology with linear, quadratic, and cubic interaction terms, achieving ARs of at least 99.5% across all instances tested. The method consistently outperforms a classical local solver across all problems. Where published results on identical problem instances are available, our method demonstrates competitive or superior performance. These results demonstrate that an appropriately engineered variational approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes at the 156-qubit scale, where naïve implementations are insufficient for good performance.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical variational optimization method for binary combinatorial problems on gate-model quantum computers, demonstrated on IBM hardware up to 156 qubits.
motivation: To solve NP-hard binary optimization problems on near-term quantum computers despite noise and limited connectivity.
method: Integrates a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based parameter updates, efficient compilation, automated error suppression, and classical post-processing for bitflip correction.
result: Achieves approximation ratios of 100% for Max-Cut on unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes and ≥99.5% for spin-glass models up to 156 qubits, outperforming classical local solvers.
conclusion: An appropriately engineered variational approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization at the 156-qubit scale.

title: A Machine-Learning Based Approach To The Evaluation Of The Critical Scaling Behavior Of Anisotropic Spin Systems
authors: Alina A. Chubarova, Ivan A. Mamonov, Marina V. Mamonova, Mikhail I. Bogachev, Pavel V. Prudnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational models adequately representing phase transitions and evaluating the critical system parameters are essential for the understanding of the properties of a wide range of materials. Here we propose a machine learning (ML)-based approach to the identification of the critical point in anisotropic spin systems. Our approach implies training of a convolutional neural network (CNN) model from the correlation matrices obtained by Monte Carlo simulations. Next, the pretrained model is employed as a fast estimator of the critical temperature, which can be extracted in several complementary ways from the CNN model inference, this way improving the robustness of the analysis. The ML-based estimates obtained in this study are in very good agreement with the reference Monte Carlo simulation results, while computational costs are about 10x lower compared to the classical thermodynamic approach.
tldr: Uses machine learning to estimate critical temperature in anisotropic spin systems from Monte Carlo correlation matrices.
motivation: Efficiently and robustly identify critical points in spin systems with lower computational cost than traditional thermodynamic methods.
method: Trains a convolutional neural network on correlation matrices from Monte Carlo simulations, then uses the trained model to estimate critical temperature via multiple inference strategies.
result: ML-based estimates agree well with reference Monte Carlo results, with about 10x reduction in computational cost.
conclusion: The proposed ML approach provides a fast and robust alternative for evaluating critical scaling behavior in anisotropic spin systems.

title: Arbitrary-Order Scattering Exceptional Points In Configurable Non-Hermitian Zero-Index Materials
authors: Yucheng Xu, Ling Yin, Yongxing Wang, Jie Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scattering exceptional points (EPs) are non-Hermitian degeneracies where the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of scattering matrices coalesce, enabling many intriguing phenomena in optical systems. Higher-order scattering EPs are particularly notable for their ultrasensitive response to perturbations, yet achieving flexible, arbitrary-order control remains challenging. Here, we propose a configurable non-Hermitian zero-index material (ZIM) network that enables arbitrary-order scattering EPs, as rigorously proved theoretically and validated numerically. Specifically, we show that in an N-port non-Hermitian ZIM network embedded with loss/gain dopants, the maximum achievable EP order is N, and the order can be flexibly tuned from 2 to N or completely eliminated by adjusting the dopants. Furthermore, we compare conventional coherent perfect absorption with absorbing EPs of different orders. Although both achieve perfect absorption of all incident waves, a second-order EP already outperforms coherent perfect absorption, and higher-order EPs provide further power-law enhancement. These findings establish a pathway toward realizing arbitrary-order EPs in open scattering systems, holding significant promise for advanced sensing applications.
tldr: This paper proposes a configurable non-Hermitian zero-index material network to realize arbitrary-order scattering exceptional points for enhanced sensing.
motivation: Higher-order exceptional points offer ultrasensitive response but achieving flexible, arbitrary-order control in open scattering systems remains challenging.
method: The authors design an N-port non-Hermitian zero-index material network with loss/gain dopants and theoretically prove that the maximum EP order equals N, tunable by adjusting dopants.
result: They demonstrate that second-order EPs already outperform coherent perfect absorption, and higher-order EPs provide further power-law enhancement in sensitivity.
conclusion: This work establishes a pathway to realize arbitrary-order EPs in open systems, with significant promise for advanced sensing applications.

title: Phase Lag Enhances Synchronization In Coupled Oscillators With Inertia
authors: Sudo Yi, Cook Hyun Kim, Heetae Kim, B. Kahng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The second-order Kuramoto model with inertia exhibits different dynamical behaviors than the first-order KM without inertia. A central difference is its lower synchronization due to the emergence of multiple synchronized clusters with different frequencies. We aim to investigate how such lowered synchronization can be improved by applying external perturbations to the system in a steady state, for example, a symmetry-breaking phase lag to a subset of oscillators. We find that this phase lag steers the primary cluster along a specific path and enables it to merge with higher-order clusters, thereby enhancing global synchronization. Our results reveal a mechanism by which controlled phase lag can improve entrainment in inertial oscillator systems, with possible implications for synchronization control in inertial oscillator networks.
tldr: This paper studies synchronization enhancement in the second-order Kuramoto model by applying a phase lag to a subset of oscillators.
motivation: The second-order Kuramoto model with inertia exhibits lower synchronization due to multiple frequency clusters; the authors aim to improve global synchronization via controlled external perturbations.
method: They introduce a symmetry-breaking phase lag to a subset of oscillators in a steady state and analyze the resulting cluster dynamics.
result: The phase lag steers the primary cluster along a specific path, enabling it to merge with higher-order clusters and thereby enhance global synchronization.
conclusion: Controlled phase lag can improve entrainment in inertial oscillator systems, with potential implications for synchronization control in networks.

title: A Survey On Rigorous Results For The Dynamics Of Periodic Fpu Chains
authors: Dario Bambusi, Andrea Carati, Alberto Maiocchi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we review some analytic results on the dynamics of the FPU system. In the first part of the paper, having in mind that the FPU Hamiltonian and the Toda Hamiltonian are close each other, we present some results on the action angle variables of the Toda system and deduce some stability properties for the dynamics of the FPU system. We first focus on the case of finitely many particles and then we study the limit [MATH]. We present also some results on the continous limit of the Toda chain showing that it is well described by a couple of KdV equations. Then we study directly the dynamics of the function interpolating the FPU system and show that the dynamics is Hamiltonian and that the Hamiltonian is very close to a function of the first three Hamiltonians of the KdV hierarchy. In the second part of the paper we present some results valid in the thermodynamic limit, according to which the time autocorrelation functions of some suitably constructed observables decay slowly implying lower bounds on the thermalization times of the system.
tldr: A survey of rigorous results on the dynamics of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) chain, focusing on stability and thermalization times.
motivation: The FPU chain is a classic model in nonlinear dynamics and statistical mechanics, and understanding its long-time behavior is fundamental.
method: The paper reviews analytic results using action-angle variables of the Toda system, continuous limits via KdV equations, and thermodynamic limit analysis.
result: Stability properties are deduced for finite chains, and lower bounds on thermalization times are obtained from slow decay of autocorrelation functions.
conclusion: The FPU system exhibits slow thermalization, with dynamics close to integrable Toda and KdV hierarchies.

title: Improved Cryogenic Photodiode Optical Biasing For Low-Noise And Low-Jitter Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
authors: Jia-Hao Hu, Wei-Jun Zhang, Wen-Shuo Yu, Yu-Ze Wang, Dong-Wei Chu, Ya-Tao Peng, Hui-Qin Yu, Pu-Sheng Yuan, Ling Wu, Li-Xing You
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate an improved optical biasing scheme for superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), which employs a cryogenic InGaAs-InP photodiode (PD) as a local bias source. It is found that, under illumination from a stable external light source, this PD generates a stable photocurrent in a cryogenic environment (~2.3 K), with fluctuations in the photocurrent primarily attributed to fluctuations in the incident optical power. Furthermore, by screening and effectively blocking stray photons leaking from the PD, which give rise to background dark counts, we have achieved an SNSPD exhibiting an ultra-low intrinsic dark count rate of 1e-4 cps. Utilizing this improved optical biasing technique, our SNSPD achieved performance comparable to that obtained under conventional electrical biasing: a system detection efficiency of 80.7%, a background dark count rate of 32.6 cps, and a minimum timing jitter of 57.5 ps. These results indicate that cryogenic-PD-based optical biasing serves as a viable, low-noise, and low-jitter alternative to traditional electrical biasing. Moreover, this work offers useful design guidance for the future development of PD-based low-noise bias sources and for the construction of all-photonic SNSPD systems tailored for high-precision quantum photonics applications.
tldr: This paper presents an improved cryogenic photodiode optical biasing scheme for SNSPDs, achieving low noise and low jitter.
motivation: To reduce noise and jitter in SNSPDs by replacing conventional electrical biasing with a cryogenic photodiode-based optical biasing source.
method: A cryogenic InGaAs-InP photodiode is used as a local bias source under stable external illumination; stray photons from the PD are screened to reduce dark counts.
result: The SNSPD achieves an ultra-low intrinsic dark count rate of 1e-4 cps, system detection efficiency of 80.7%, background dark count rate of 32.6 cps, and minimum timing jitter of 57.5 ps.
conclusion: Cryogenic-PD-based optical biasing is a viable low-noise, low-jitter alternative to electrical biasing, useful for high-precision quantum photonics applications.

title: Normal Forms Of Unidirectional Coupling In Quasi-phase-matched non-Hermitian Systems
authors: Kestutis Staliunas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal conditions for unidirectional coupling in quasi-phase-matched non-Hermitian systems are analyzed for both autonomous and externally driven configurations. The quasi-phase-matched coupling mechanism is due to periodic modulation of the real and imaginary parts of the coupling interface, which results in unequal coupling coefficients between interacting waves. The conventional parity-time (PT) symmetry theory suggests that the strongest unidirectionality should occur exactly at the exceptional point (EP). We show that this expectation is generally incorrect, as the optimum is shifted away from the EP depending on the detuning from exact quasi-phase-matching resonance. We formulate a unified two-mode description for autonomous and driven systems, and derive the corresponding normal forms near the shifted singularities associated with the EPs.
tldr: This paper studies unidirectional coupling in quasi-phase-matched non-Hermitian systems, focusing on optimal conditions away from exceptional points.
motivation: To correct the common assumption that the strongest unidirectionality occurs at the exceptional point in PT-symmetric systems, and to provide a unified description for autonomous and driven configurations.
method: The authors analyze a two-mode model with periodic modulation of real and imaginary parts of the coupling, deriving normal forms near shifted singularities associated with exceptional points.
result: The optimum for unidirectional coupling is shifted away from the exceptional point depending on detuning from quasi-phase-matching resonance.
conclusion: The findings provide a more accurate framework for designing unidirectional couplers in non-Hermitian systems.

title: On The Conditional Equivalence Of Phase Retrieval Algorithms
authors: Andreas D\"opp Jakob Schroeder
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase retrieval - recovering a complex-valued field from intensity measurements - is typically solved using variants of the Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) algorithm, understood as alternating projections between measurement planes. Meanwhile, modern computational imaging increasingly relies on gradient-based optimization and automatic differentiation. Here we show that these two approaches are mathematically identical: the GS magnitude replacement step is exactly a unit gradient descent step on an amplitude least-squares loss. This equivalence enables seamless integration of classical phase retrieval with differentiable physics pipelines. We further identify two complementary probabilistic interpretations of this equivalence: globally, the amplitude loss is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian amplitude noise; locally, each projection step arises as a Bayesian update with the propagated field as prior. The local view provides qualitative guidance for relaxation in iterative phase retrieval.
tldr: This paper shows that the Gerchberg-Saxton phase retrieval algorithm is equivalent to gradient descent on an amplitude least-squares loss, enabling integration with differentiable physics pipelines.
motivation: Phase retrieval is typically solved with alternating projections, while modern imaging uses gradient-based optimization; the paper aims to unify these approaches.
method: The authors prove that the magnitude replacement step in Gerchberg-Saxton is exactly a unit gradient descent step on an amplitude least-squares loss, and provide probabilistic interpretations.
result: The equivalence allows classical phase retrieval to be seamlessly integrated into differentiable physics frameworks, with both global (Gaussian noise) and local (Bayesian update) probabilistic interpretations.
conclusion: The work bridges classical and modern phase retrieval methods, offering practical guidance for algorithm design and relaxation.

title: Variations On Majorization Of Vectors And Connections To Determinantal Inequalities
authors: Shaun Fallat, Samir Mondal, Hristo Sendov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Majorization is a fundamental tool for comparing vectors, with connections to convexity, doubly stochastic matrices, eigenvalues, singular values, and zeros of polynomials. In matrix analysis, it plays a central role in the study of eigenvalue inequalities, particularly those arising from classical determinantal inequalities such as those attributed to Hadamard and Fischer in the context of positive semidefinite matrices. A result of Fischer and Holbrook shows that equality in the Hardy--Littlewood--P\'olya theorem for non-affine convex functions is closely linked to block structure in the associated doubly stochastic transformations. Motivated by this, we introduce [MATH]-majorization, a structured extension of majorization that respects prescribed block decompositions of vectors. This framework naturally corresponds to block diagonal doubly stochastic matrices and provides a refinement of the classical Hardy--Littlewood--P\'olya and Rado theorem. We show that such transformations are precisely the linear operators that preserve [MATH]-majorization, and we extend fundamental constructions such as [MATH]-transforms and convex combinations to this setting. In an application, we study the eigenvalue relations associated with the principal submatrices of positive definite matrices. Classical majorization does not, in general, capture determinantal inequalities such as those of Koteljanskii, whereas [MATH]-majorization provides a natural framework for structured comparisons of eigenvalue vectors. This leads to new insights into the interplay between majorization theory, determinantal inequalities, and spectral properties of matrices.
tldr: This paper introduces a structured extension of majorization called M-majorization, which respects block decompositions of vectors, and applies it to determinantal inequalities for positive definite matrices.
motivation: Classical majorization does not capture certain determinantal inequalities like Koteljanskii's inequality, motivating a refined framework that respects block structure.
method: The authors define M-majorization based on block diagonal doubly stochastic matrices, characterize the linear operators that preserve it, and extend classical majorization constructions such as M-transforms and convex combinations.
result: M-majorization provides a natural framework for comparing eigenvalue vectors of principal submatrices, leading to new insights into determinantal inequalities and spectral properties.
conclusion: The work bridges majorization theory and matrix analysis, offering a structured tool for eigenvalue comparisons that classical majorization cannot handle.

title: Data-driven Methods For Computation Of Optimal Linear Response In High-dimensional Dynamical Systems
authors: Gary Froyland, Dimitrios Giannakis, Nicholas Peters
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a data-driven framework for estimating optimal linear response of nonlinear dynamical systems. Our approach is based on kernel-smoothed approximations of the transfer/Koopman operators of the system, built from possibly high-dimensional observations along trajectories. Combining these operator approximations with the theory developed in [Antown et al. (2018), J. Stat. Phys., 170(6), 1051-1087], we formulate a computationally tractable optimization problem for the optimal infinitesimal perturbation realising any desired manipulation of the spectrum. We also introduce a notion of optimal-response vector fields for visualising, and physically interpreting, the system's response to the optimal perturbation under arbitrary observations. Our focus is on finding perturbations that optimally increase the frequency or optimally suppress the decay of correlations of almost-cycles or almost-invariant sets associated with the eigenvalues of the kernel-smoothed transfer operator. We illustrate our approach with applications to low-dimensional periodic and chaotic systems, as well as a high-dimensional example involving the El Nino Southern Oscillation in a comprehensive Earth system model. In these examples our approach discovers nontrivial optimal perturbations of the system, which are post hoc natural and consistent with the desired dynamical objectives.
tldr: A data-driven framework for computing optimal linear response in high-dimensional dynamical systems using kernel-smoothed approximations of transfer/Koopman operators.
motivation: To develop a computationally tractable method for finding optimal perturbations that manipulate the spectrum of nonlinear dynamical systems, with applications to climate and other complex systems.
method: Kernel-smoothed approximations of transfer/Koopman operators from trajectory data are combined with optimization theory to find optimal infinitesimal perturbations.
result: The method discovers nontrivial optimal perturbations for low-dimensional chaotic systems and a high-dimensional Earth system model (El Niño Southern Oscillation).
conclusion: The approach provides a practical way to compute optimal linear response and visualize response vector fields, with potential for climate and geophysical applications.

title: Degrees Of Freedom Of Over-the-Air Computation Over A Mimo Gaussian Network With Two Transmitters And Two Receivers
authors: Yong Dong, Hua Sun, Syed A. Jafar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fundamental limits of over-the-air computation (AirComp) are explored in a two-transmitter, two-receiver MIMO Gaussian network, where both receivers demand the same aggregation of source symbols originating at the two transmitters. An AirComp degrees of freedom (ACDoF) metric is defined, constrained by an asymptotic mean-squared error threshold. For a generic MIMO setting where the two transmitters are equipped with [MATH] antennas, and the two receivers with [MATH] antennas, the AirComp DoF value is shown to be almost surely equal to [MATH]. For SISO settings results are extended beyond generic channels to arbitrary channel realizations. For finite signal-to-noise ratio(SNR) settings, an iterative alternating optimization algorithm is explored.
tldr: This paper studies the degrees of freedom of over-the-air computation in a MIMO Gaussian network with two transmitters and two receivers.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of over-the-air computation, a technique for distributed function computation over wireless channels, in a MIMO setting.
method: The authors define an AirComp degrees of freedom (ACDoF) metric and analyze it for generic MIMO channels using information-theoretic tools, and for SISO channels for arbitrary realizations. They also propose an iterative alternating optimization algorithm for finite SNR.
result: For generic MIMO channels, the ACDoF is almost surely equal to min(M, N) where M and N are the number of antennas at transmitters and receivers respectively.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of the ACDoF for the considered network, extending results to arbitrary SISO channels and finite SNR.

title: Information Rate Decomposition For Noisy Nanopore Channels With Geometric Duplication
authors: Emanuele Viterbo Brendon Mcbain
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies information rates of noisy duplication channels with memory, motivated by nanopore DNA sequencing. In nanopore sequencing, the measured signal is affected by both inter-symbol interference (ISI), caused by multiple DNA bases residing in the pore, and random sample duplications, where variable translocation speed causes each base to generate a random number of samples. These two effects make direct theoretical analysis difficult. To address this, we derive a new decomposition of the information rate into two interpretable terms: one associated with the intrinsic memory of an auxiliary ISI channel, and another that captures the uncertainty in the segment boundaries caused by random duplications. This decomposition separates the dominant channel distortions and replaces the direct analysis of the full channel with two more readily interpretable components. We then study the second term through a soft alignment functional closely related to Soft-DTW, which enables strong AEP results and an alternative proof of the Markov-constrained coding theorem based on strong information stability. Finally, we develop a lower bound on the information rate that depends on the distribution of jump distances between adjacent nanopore levels. This bound gives a simple geometric explanation of channel synchronisability and provides a tractable framework for computing achievable rates of Oxford nanopore sequencers.
tldr: This paper studies information rates of noisy duplication channels with memory, motivated by nanopore DNA sequencing, and proposes a decomposition into an ISI term and a duplication uncertainty term.
motivation: Nanopore DNA sequencing suffers from inter-symbol interference and random sample duplications, making theoretical analysis of information rates difficult.
method: The authors derive a decomposition of the information rate into two interpretable terms: one for intrinsic memory of an auxiliary ISI channel and another for segment boundary uncertainty due to duplications, analyzed via a soft alignment functional related to Soft-DTW.
result: The decomposition enables strong AEP results and an alternative proof of the Markov-constrained coding theorem; a lower bound on the information rate is derived based on jump distances between nanopore levels.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable framework for computing achievable rates of Oxford nanopore sequencers, with a geometric explanation of channel synchronisability.

title: Multiscale Nudging: From Macroscopic Observations To Microscopic Dynamics
authors: Liyao Lyu, Xinyue Yu, Hayden Schaeffer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a measure-based nudging framework for assimilating macroscopic observations into microscopic mean-field particle dynamics. The central difficulty is a representation mismatch: the forecast is a labeled particle system, while the observations specify only a smoothed, permutation-invariant density. To address this mismatch, we define the forecast-observation discrepancy as a quadratic functional on probability measures after applying the same smoothing operator used by the observation process. The Wasserstein gradient of this functional induces a transport velocity on state space, which yields a particle-level correction without constructing particle-to-particle matching, linearizing the dynamics, or estimating ensemble covariances. For a fixed observation scale, we prove well-posedness of the assimilated McKean-Vlasov dynamics and propagation of chaos for the interacting particle approximation. Under exact smoothed observations and an observability condition at the kernel scale, we establish an [MATH]-stability estimate showing exponential decay up to a bias floor controlled by model misspecification. Numerical experiments on linear, bimodal, chaotic, kinetic, and collective-motion systems demonstrate that the method can recover macroscopic structure from incomplete density-level observations.
tldr: A measure-based nudging framework for assimilating macroscopic density observations into microscopic particle dynamics.
motivation: To correct representation mismatch between labeled particle forecasts and smoothed, permutation-invariant observations without explicit particle matching or covariance estimation.
method: Defines a quadratic discrepancy functional on probability measures using the observation smoothing operator, then uses its Wasserstein gradient to derive a transport velocity for particle-level correction.
result: Proves well-posedness of assimilated McKean-Vlasov dynamics, propagation of chaos, and exponential stability up to a bias floor under exact observations and an observability condition.
conclusion: The method effectively recovers macroscopic structure from incomplete density observations across various dynamical systems.

title: Mutual Information Optimization Via K-Recursion And Automatic Differentiation For Linear Gaussian Wireless Networks
authors: Na Siqi Tadashi Wadayama
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a differentiable framework for end-to-end mutual information (MI) optimization over linear Gaussian directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). The framework targets network-wide design under global constraints, such as a total transmit power budget, and covers MIMO precoding, amplify-and-forward relays, RIS-aided channels, and branching/merging topologies within a common linear Gaussian model. Its core ingredient is a that analytically propagates all node-pair covariances along the DAG in topological order, including non-adjacent cross-covariances that are necessary for correctly handling branching and merging paths. The resulting covariances yield a closed-form log-determinant expression for the end-to-end MI as a smooth function of the controllable factors. Complex-valued reverse-mode automatic differentiation on this K-recursion then returns the exact Wirtinger gradient at every controllable factor in a single backward sweep, and projected gradient ascent (PGA) is used to maximize the MI under the global constraints. Because no closed-form gradient expression per topology is required, the same topology-agnostic implementation applies to any linear Gaussian DAG. A single topology-agnostic implementation is applied to four representative DAG classes: single-link MIMO, a diamond DAG, a two-hop AF relay, and input-covariance shaping. The same implementation reaches the classical water-filling optimum in the settings where it is available and yields MI improvements in non-single-link topologies without using topology-specific gradient formulas. A further experiment on a multi-layer Gaussian network (11 nodes, 5 layers) illustrates applicability to nontrivial multi-layer topologies for which no closed-form gradient is available.
tldr: A differentiable framework for mutual information optimization in linear Gaussian wireless networks using K-recursion and automatic differentiation.
motivation: To enable end-to-end mutual information optimization over arbitrary linear Gaussian directed acyclic graphs without topology-specific gradient formulas.
method: Propagates all node-pair covariances along the DAG via K-recursion, computes MI via log-determinant, and uses automatic differentiation for exact gradients.
result: Achieves classical water-filling optimum in single-link MIMO and improves MI in non-single-link topologies; demonstrated on diamond, two-hop AF relay, and multi-layer networks.
conclusion: The topology-agnostic framework effectively optimizes MI under global constraints for a wide class of linear Gaussian networks.

title: N-Player Binary Games With Unidirectional Dependencies: Cycle Robustness And Induced Indifference
authors: Jose Maria Sanchez-Saez, Nana Odishelidze, Francisco Criado-Aldeanueva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The present study provides a closed-form characterisation of Nash equilibria in N-player binary games with unidirectional dependencies. While general network games are PPAD-complete, prior work has established that trees or paths admit polynomial-time solutions via dynamic programming. We provide a deterministic characterisation for the subclass of directed cycle graphical games, demonstrating that non-zero boundary incentives linearize the topology into a feed-forward propagation. Under this Robust Incentive Structure, resolution is achieved in O(N) time: strict dominance guarantees a unique equilibrium; in its absence, pure strategy equilibria are governed by the Parity Condition, while a unique fully mixed equilibrium is guaranteed via induced payoff indifference. For non-robust regimes, we deliver branching rules. The transition-matrix formulation evaluates the search tree size beforehand. This transparency enables the inverse design of target equilibria in circular networks, making explicit the mechanics that remain opaque in numerical solvers.
tldr: This paper provides a closed-form characterization of Nash equilibria in N-player binary games with unidirectional dependencies, focusing on directed cycle graphical games.
motivation: General network games are computationally hard (PPAD-complete), but certain subclasses like trees admit efficient solutions. The authors aim to extend tractable analysis to directed cycles.
method: They develop a deterministic characterization using a robust incentive structure that linearizes the cycle into feed-forward propagation, and provide a transition-matrix formulation to evaluate search tree size.
result: Under robust incentives, equilibria are found in O(N) time; strict dominance yields a unique equilibrium, otherwise pure strategy equilibria follow a parity condition and a unique fully mixed equilibrium exists via induced indifference.
conclusion: The work enables inverse design of target equilibria in circular networks, making the mechanics transparent compared to numerical solvers.

title: The Economics Of Proof-of-Useful-Work
authors: Rafael Pass
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof-of-work (PoW) blockchains rely on computational expenditure to secure a ledger supporting a native cryptocurrency. In existing systems such as Bitcoin, this expenditure is intentionally useless: the computation secures consensus but produces no external economic output. An emerging alternative -- proof of useful work (PoUW) -- enables the same computation to simultaneously secure the blockchain and generate economically valuable output. However, PoUW is often criticized on economic grounds: if the work is useful, attackers might be "paid to attack," potentially weakening security. We develop a competitive-equilibrium model of a PoUW blockchain in which compute can be allocated across pure mining, pure useful work -- instantiated as machine-learning inference -- or "duplex" work that produces both with computational overheads. We provide a complete closed-form characterization of equilibrium allocations and prices as a function of the duplex overheads and a single economic parameter -- the token-inference ratio -- measuring token adoption relative to the inference market. This characterization reveals three regimes: "Bitconia," in which the economy reduces to classical PoW; "Fortessia," in which duplex replaces mining, increasing security while useful output remains unchanged; and "Duplexia," in which token rewards subsidize inference, lowering prices and expanding inference supply. Contrary to the common strawman argument, PoUW does not make attacks economically cheap: once equilibrium prices are taken into account, the economic cost of a majority attack remains tied to the block reward. Moreover, in Duplexia, block rewards act as rebates on inference prices, generating additional socially useful computation that would not arise without the blockchain -- an expansion monotonically increasing in token adoption and technological efficiency.
tldr: This paper models the economics of proof-of-useful-work blockchains, analyzing equilibrium allocations and security implications.
motivation: To address economic criticisms that proof-of-useful-work may weaken blockchain security by allowing attackers to be 'paid to attack'.
method: Develops a competitive-equilibrium model where compute is allocated across pure mining, useful work (ML inference), or duplex work, and derives closed-form equilibrium conditions.
result: Identifies three regimes (Bitconia, Fortessia, Duplexia) and shows that PoUW does not make attacks economically cheap; block rewards can subsidize useful computation.
conclusion: PoUW can enhance security and generate socially useful computation without compromising economic attack costs.

title: Blockchain Infrastructure For Intelligent Cyber--Physical--Social Systems:Post-Quantum Security, Interoperability, And Trustworthy Data Economies In The Era Of Embodied Ai
authors: Song Guo, Huawei Huang, Dongping Liu, Aoyu Zhang, Luyao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The deployment of embodied artificial intelligence via world-model-based robotics presents a transformative opportunity for blockchain infrastructure, establishing urgent demand for trustworthy data provenance, cross-organizational governance, and incentive-compatible sharing across decentralized ecosystems. Simultaneously, quantum computing advances recognized by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics and the Turing Award threaten the cryptographic primitives securing these data economies, creating an interdependent imperative: long-lived verification for embodied AI depends on crypto-agile architectures capable of withstanding quantum adversaries. This tutorial examines blockchain as the coordination layer bridging this dual transition, from financial substrate to foundational Cyber-Physical-Social Systems infrastructure that simultaneously secures against quantum cryptanalysis and enables scalable, trustworthy data economies. The session opens with an immersive AWS Braket demonstration engaging participants with superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom hardware to assess cryptographic threat timelines and witness ECDSA-to-post-quantum signature transitions. Five integrated modules progress from embodied AI and world-model requirements through quantum hardware reality and evidence-based security migration, to scalable cross-shard architectures via BrokerChain protocols, trustworthy data economies implementing Croissant metadata standards and robotic learning provenance, and industry ecosystem integration for multi-modal cloud deployment. By bridging quantum hardware realities with embodied AI data requirements, this tutorial charts blockchain as unified infrastructure for next-generation decentralized intelligent environments, providing open-source frameworks and roadmaps for architecting quantum-resistant, interoperable, and data-trustworthy systems.
tldr: A tutorial on blockchain infrastructure for cyber-physical-social systems, focusing on post-quantum security and embodied AI data economies.
motivation: To address the need for trustworthy data provenance and crypto-agile architectures in decentralized systems facing quantum threats.
method: The paper presents a tutorial with five modules covering embodied AI, quantum hardware, post-quantum signature migration, cross-shard blockchain protocols, and data economy standards.
result: It provides open-source frameworks and roadmaps for quantum-resistant, interoperable blockchain systems.
conclusion: Blockchain can serve as unified infrastructure for next-generation decentralized intelligent environments, but the work is a high-level tutorial without novel technical contributions.

title: Empirical Evaluation Of Large Language Models For Migration Of Code Fragments To Post-Quantum Cryptography
authors: Javier Pallar\'es de Bonrostro, Ana I. Gonz\'alez-Tablas, Mar\'ia Isabel Gonz\'alez Vasco
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) requires not only replacing vulnerable cryptographic primitives, but also refactoring the surrounding software logic. While existing PQC migration frameworks provide organizational guidance, practical code-level remediation remains largely manual and error-prone. This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can be trained to assist in the migration of pre-quantum cryptographic code fragments to post-quantum counterparts while preserving functional correctness. To this end, we introduce a reproducible experimental framework built around a synthetic dataset of 800 paired Python code fragments covering six cryptographic families and combined multi-primitive cases. Each pair is validated through category-specific functional tests, enabling both dataset quality control and objective evaluation of model-generated migrations. Four models are assessed: GPT-4.1 in a zero-shot setting, and fine-tuned versions of GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4.1-mini, and CodeLlama-7B-Instruct. The results show that domain-specific fine-tuning is essential for reliable cryptographic migration. The fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini model achieves the best overall performance, with a mean static similarity of 0.9072 and a dynamic functional correctness rate of 92.5%, substantially outperforming the zero-shot baseline. A complementary validation on six open-source repositories further shows that the approach can produce useful migrations in localized cryptographic modules, while also revealing limitations in larger projects with complex dependencies and cross-module interactions. These findings suggest that fine-tuned LLMs can serve as practical components in future crypto-agile migration pipelines, provided they are coupled with automated verification and dependency-aware validation.
tldr: Evaluates LLMs for migrating classical cryptographic code to post-quantum cryptography, focusing on functional correctness.
motivation: The transition to post-quantum cryptography requires automated code migration to reduce manual effort and errors.
method: A synthetic dataset of 800 paired Python code fragments is used to fine-tune and evaluate LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama) on migration tasks with functional tests.
result: Fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini achieves 92.5% functional correctness and 0.9072 static similarity, outperforming zero-shot baselines.
conclusion: Fine-tuned LLMs can assist in PQC migration but require automated verification and dependency-aware validation for complex projects.
