title: No-Harm Physics-Informed Inverse Learning With Residual-Calibrated Uncertainty
authors: Ronald Katende
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed learning is increasingly used for partial differential equation (PDE)-governed inverse problems, but its reliability remains difficult to certify. This paper develops a no-harm certification-and-selection framework for physics-informed inverse learning. A learned reconstruction is accepted only when its residual-calibrated radius is no worse than the baseline radius, namely when $[MATH]$otherwise, the method returns the baseline. The certificate combines data, physics, boundary or initial-condition, and optimization residuals. Under a conditional stability estimate, these residuals yield an a posteriori reconstruction-error bound and a deterministic uncertainty radius. A high-probability certificate is also derived for physics residuals estimated from independent random collocation points. Numerical tests on Poisson source recovery, inverse heat reconstruction, limited-angle tomography, elliptic coefficient identification, and stochastic residual validation show that the selector accepts certified improvements, rejects shifted, hallucinated, or unfinished candidates, and becomes conservative in strongly ill-posed regimes. The framework is therefore a certification-and-selection layer, not another reconstruction architecture.
tldr: A no-harm certification-and-selection framework for physics-informed inverse learning that accepts reconstructions only when their residual-calibrated uncertainty is no worse than a baseline.
motivation: Physics-informed learning for PDE-governed inverse problems lacks reliability certification, making it difficult to trust learned reconstructions.
method: The framework combines data, physics, boundary, and optimization residuals into an a posteriori error bound and deterministic uncertainty radius, and uses a conditional stability estimate to certify reconstructions.
result: Numerical tests on Poisson source recovery, inverse heat reconstruction, limited-angle tomography, and elliptic coefficient identification show the selector accepts certified improvements and rejects shifted or hallucinated candidates.
conclusion: The framework provides a certification-and-selection layer that can be added to any reconstruction method, improving reliability without requiring a new architecture.

title: The Synthesis-Sequencing Channel For DNA-based Data Storage
authors: Keshav Goyal, Samuel Pearson, Jo\~ao Ribeiro, Serge Kas Hanna
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study the synthesis-sequencing channel, a two-stage model for DNA-based data storage that jointly captures synthesis and sequencing effects. The synthesis-sequencing channel provides a more nuanced and realistic model of the DNA storage process compared to prior work, as it distinguishes between physical coverage after synthesis and sequencing coverage after readout, relaxes the assumption of independent errors across reads, and naturally induces coverage bias through the composition of synthesis and sequencing stages. We establish the information-theoretic capacity of this channel by deriving matching converse and achievability bounds for the case where synthesis and sequencing errors are modeled by binary symmetric channels with possibly different error probabilities, under mild assumptions on the channel parameters. Our results reveal multiple trade-offs between physical coverage, synthesis errors, sequencing coverage, and sequencing errors that influence the maximum achievable rate for reliable data storage.
tldr: This paper introduces a synthesis-sequencing channel model for DNA-based data storage and derives its information-theoretic capacity.
motivation: DNA storage is a promising archival medium, but realistic channel models are needed to understand fundamental limits.
method: The authors model the storage process as a two-stage channel with binary symmetric errors and derive matching converse and achievability bounds.
result: The capacity is characterized, revealing trade-offs between physical coverage, synthesis errors, sequencing coverage, and sequencing errors.
conclusion: The results provide theoretical guidance for designing reliable DNA storage systems.

authors: Martijn Brehm, Yuval Ishai, Nicolas Resch
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We continue the study of {\em fast} functions, computable by linear-size circuits, that share useful properties of random functions. Motivated by cryptographic applications, we generalize and improve on previous results in this area, obtaining the following results: - For any constant [MATH], we construct a fast [MATH]-wise independent hash function with algebraic degree [MATH] (over [MATH]), simultaneously optimizing both asymptotic circuit size and degree. - We simplify and improve a recent construction (ITCS 2026) of a family of fast codes with fast duals, both meeting the Gilbert-Varshamov bound. Unlike the previous construction, our construction has negligible failure probability, can accommodate general fields and rates, supports a systematic encoding, and admits fast universal encoders. - We strengthen the above to support stronger random-like properties, such as optimal combinatorial list-decoding. This is achieved by constructing, for any constant [MATH], a family of fast linear functions that map any [MATH] linearly independent inputs to uniform and statistically independent outputs. Prior to our work, this was only known for [MATH]. We demonstrate the usefulness of the above results to cryptography. This includes the first nontrivial protocols for perfectly secure multiparty computation whose circuit complexity scales linearly with the number of parties, as well as protocols for computing encrypted matrix-vector products with optimal asymptotic circuit complexity.

motivation: To design functions computable by linear-size circuits that mimic random functions, improving efficiency in cryptographic protocols.

result: Achieves optimal asymptotic circuit size and degree for hash functions, codes meeting the Gilbert-Varshamov bound with negligible failure probability, and supports stronger random-like properties.
conclusion: These constructions enable the first nontrivial perfectly secure MPC protocols with linear circuit complexity and optimal encrypted matrix-vector products.

title: Sort, Partition, Randomize: Optimal Binary Hypothesis Testing Under Local Differential Privacy
authors: Elena Ghazi, Jawad Nasser, Flavio Calmon, Ibrahim Issa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study optimal design of [MATH]-locally differentially private mechanisms for binary hypothesis testing. Each observation is drawn from one of two known distributions [MATH] on a finite alphabet of size [MATH], privatized by a mechanism [MATH], and then used to infer which distribution generated the data. We measure testing utility using an [MATH]-divergence, including total variation, KL, and hockey-stick divergences, between the two induced output distributions. Previous work established structural properties of optimal mechanisms, but only yielded exponential-time algorithms. We prove a sharp structure: for every [MATH] and every [MATH]-divergence objective, after sorting the alphabet by likelihood ratio, there exists an optimal mechanism that partitions the sorted alphabet into contiguous blocks and applies randomized response to the block label. We call this class Sort-Partition-Randomize (SPR). This characterization yields an exact dynamic program that computes an optimal mechanism in [MATH] time, and more generally in [MATH] time with an [MATH]-output budget. Our results make it possible to efficiently compute and characterize the exact optimum across the full privacy range, beyond asymptotic privacy regimes.

motivation: Designing optimal privacy-preserving mechanisms for hypothesis testing is important but previous algorithms were exponential-time; a more efficient characterization is needed.
method: The authors prove that for any f-divergence, an optimal mechanism sorts the alphabet by likelihood ratio, partitions it into contiguous blocks, and applies randomized response to the block label, leading to a dynamic programming algorithm.
result: The Sort-Partition-Randomize (SPR) class characterizes optimal mechanisms, and an exact dynamic program computes the optimum in O(k^3) time, or O(k^2) with an output budget.
conclusion: The work provides a complete, efficient solution to optimal binary hypothesis testing under local differential privacy across the full privacy range.

authors: Zhihao Chen, Chun Sum Brian Pang, Meng Yang, Yuxin Wang, Huaiyuan Wang, He Zheng, Kun Jiang, Bruce A. Davidson, Ilya Elfimov, George A. Sawatzky, Andrea Damascelli, Ke Zou, And Zhi Gang Cheng

result: Observation of percolative stripe order that correlates with superconducting properties.
conclusion: Stripe order and percolation play a key role in the unconventional superconductivity of KTaO3-based systems.

title: Anomalies In The Thermal Conductivity Of The Honeycomb Antiferromagnet ${\mathrm{MnPS}}_{3}$
authors: Jian Yan, Hiromu Okamoto, Hiroki Yoshida, Hikaru Takeda, Xuan Luo, Yuping Sun, Jun-Ichi Yamaura, And Minoru Yamashita

Intrinsic two-dimensional magnets serve as a good platform to explore collective, charge-neutral, and low-energy excitations. method: Thermal conductivity measurements on MnPS3 single crystals.
result: Observed anomalies in thermal conductivity attributed to magnon-phonon interactions or spin fluctuations.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into low-energy excitations in 2D antiferromagnets but have no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Phase Transitions And Electrical Conductivity Of Selenium Disulfide At High Pressure
authors: Huixin Hu, Israel Osmond, Calum Strain, Hannah A. Shuttleworth, Callum R. Stevens, Andrew Huxley, Mikhail A. Kuzovnikov, Federico A. Gorelli, Eugene Gregoryanz, Miriam Peña-Alvarez, Philip Dalladay-Simpson, And Ross T. Howie

motivation: To explore the high-pressure behavior of interchalcogen compounds, which are less studied than pure sulfur or selenium.
method: Diamond anvil cell experiments combined with electrical conductivity measurements and structural characterization.
result: Observed pressure-induced phase transitions and changes in electrical conductivity in selenium disulfide.
conclusion: The high-pressure properties of selenium disulfide reveal complex behavior, but the work is primarily a materials science study without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Simplified Approach For Atomistic Modeling Of Magnetic Nanostructures By Scaling The Lattice Constant
authors: A. W. Teixeira, D. Altbir, S. Castillo-Sepúlveda, R. M. Corona, D. Laroze, And V. L. Carvalho-Santos

Author(s): A. W. Teixeira, D. Altbir, S. Castillo-Sepúlveda, R. M. Corona, D. Laroze, and V. L. Carvalho-Santos

Computational simulations are an important tool for understanding the magnetic properties of nanostructures that complement both experimental and analytical techniques. Among the different numerical techniques, micromagnetism offers tools for large systems; however, it presents difficulties when dea…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 224415] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a simplified computational method for atomistic modeling of magnetic nanostructures by scaling the lattice constant.
motivation: Atomistic simulations of magnetic nanostructures are computationally expensive; the authors aim to reduce cost while preserving accuracy.
method: They propose scaling the lattice constant to reduce the number of atoms, and validate the approach by comparing with full atomistic and micromagnetic simulations.
result: The scaled lattice constant method reproduces key magnetic properties (e.g., hysteresis, domain structure) with significantly lower computational cost.
conclusion: The method offers a practical trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for modeling large magnetic nanostructures.

title: Quantum Tunneling Driven Giant Electric Field Gradients In Plasmonic Cavities
authors: Chao Meng, Zhonglin Xie, Yueweiying Wang, Fanfan Lu, Ting Mei, And Wending Zhang

[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235108] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies quantum tunneling in plasmonic cavities and its effect on electric field gradients, observed via multipolar Raman scattering.
motivation: To understand how quantum tunneling affects extreme nanofocusing and field gradients in plasmonic cavities.
method: The authors use a plasmonic cavity to drive multipolar Raman scattering of asymmetric thiobenzonitrile and analyze the quadrupole-to-dipole transition.
result: Quantum tunneling suppresses extreme nanofocusing but significantly enhances the electric field gradient.
conclusion: The enhanced field gradient due to quantum tunneling can be exploited for sensing or spectroscopy applications.

title: Signatures Of Kondo-lattice Behavior In The Two-dimensional Ferromagnet ${\mathrm{Fe}}_{3}{\mathrm{GeTe}}_{2}$
authors: Carmen Rubio-Verdú And Katharina J. Franke

[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235410] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Kondo-lattice behavior in a 2D ferromagnet using STM/STS, focusing on magnetic interactions rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the microscopic magnetic interactions in Fe3GeTe2, a van der Waals magnet with debated magnetic properties.
method: Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy at 1.1 K to map low-energy electronic states on the surface.
result: Observed signatures of Kondo-lattice behavior, indicating coupling between localized magnetic moments and conduction electrons.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into the magnetic interactions in Fe3GeTe2, but are not directly relevant to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Impact Of Multiband Effects On non-Fermi-liquid Transport Phenomena In Bilayer Nickelates
authors: Seiichiro Onari, Daisuke Inoue, Rina Tazai, Youichi Yamakawa, And Hiroshi Kontani

[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245110] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies non-Fermi-liquid transport in bilayer nickelates, focusing on multiband effects and superconductivity.
motivation: To understand the anomalous transport properties observed in recently discovered high-temperature superconducting bilayer nickelates.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling and analysis of multiband electronic structure to explain non-Fermi-liquid behaviors such as T-linear resistivity and positive Hall coefficient.
result: They find that multiband effects are crucial for reproducing the observed transport anomalies.
conclusion: Multiband correlations play a key role in the non-Fermi-liquid transport and superconductivity in bilayer nickelates.

title: Valley-dependent Electron-phonon Scattering In Thermoelectric Semimetal ${\mathrm{Ta}}_{2}{\mathrm{PdSe}}_{6}$
authors: Masayuki Ochi, Hitoshi Mori, And Akitoshi Nakano
abstract:
Author(s): Masayuki Ochi, Hitoshi Mori, and Akitoshi Nakano

Quasi-one-dimensional transition-metal chalcogenide [MATH] is a promising thermoelectric semimetal due to the strong electron-hole asymmetry in the carrier lifetime. However, the microscopic origin of such a strong asymmetry remains unclear. In this study, we theoreti…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245112] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies valley-dependent electron-phonon scattering in a thermoelectric semimetal, focusing on carrier lifetime asymmetry.
motivation: To understand the microscopic origin of strong electron-hole asymmetry in carrier lifetime in Ta2PdSe6, which is important for thermoelectric performance.
method: First-principles calculations and Boltzmann transport theory to compute electron-phonon scattering rates and carrier lifetimes.
result: Valley-dependent scattering leads to significantly different lifetimes for electrons and holes, explaining the observed asymmetry.
conclusion: The valley-dependent electron-phonon scattering is the key mechanism behind the thermoelectric properties of Ta2PdSe6.

title: Biased Continuous-time Random Walks With Asymmetric Waiting-time Distributions As A Model Of Anomalous Diffusion In The Presence Of Drift
authors: Guohua Li, Andrey G. Cherstvy, Wenya Guo, Hong Zhang, Ting Liu, Wendong Pu, And Ralf Metzler
abstract:
Author(s): Guohua Li, Andrey G. Cherstvy, Wenya Guo, Hong Zhang, Ting Liu, Wendong Pu, and Ralf Metzler

Mathematical models of diffusion based on stochastic processes of the type of continuous-time random walks (CTRWs) are widely used for the description of various transport characteristics in complex media. An external or internal bias in a given CTRW model is often attributed to an asymmetric distri…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064116] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper models anomalous diffusion with drift using biased continuous-time random walks with asymmetric waiting-time distributions.
motivation: To understand transport in complex media where external bias leads to asymmetric waiting times and anomalous diffusion.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of CTRW with asymmetric waiting-time distributions and drift, deriving mean squared displacement and other transport characteristics.
result: The model captures subdiffusive, superdiffusive, and normal diffusion regimes depending on the waiting-time distribution parameters and bias strength.
conclusion: Biased CTRWs with asymmetric waiting times provide a versatile framework for describing anomalous diffusion in the presence of drift.

title: Reinforcement Learning For Chemotherapy Scheduling In A Stochastic Tumor Evolution Model

We present a [MATH]-learning framework for optimizing chemotherapy dosing schedules in a stochastic finite-cell model of tumor evolution under drug-induced selection. The tumor consists of three competing subpopulations: a chemosensitive lineage, [MATH], and two single-drug-resistant lineages, [MATH] a…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064404] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: Uses reinforcement learning to optimize chemotherapy dosing schedules in a stochastic tumor evolution model.
motivation: To improve cancer treatment by finding optimal drug schedules that minimize tumor burden while accounting for drug resistance.
method: Applies Q-learning, a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm, to a stochastic finite-cell model of tumor evolution with three competing subpopulations.
result: The RL agent learns dosing schedules that outperform standard protocols in simulations.
conclusion: Reinforcement learning is a promising tool for personalized chemotherapy scheduling, but further validation is needed.

title: Exchange Monte Carlo For Continuous-space Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Xun Zhao And Synge Todo
abstract:
Author(s): Xun Zhao and Synge Todo

We present an exchange Monte Carlo (EMC) method designed for application in continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations at finite temperature. Traditional PIMC methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, particularly when measuring observables affected by pa…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065304] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an exchange Monte Carlo method for continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo simulations to reduce autocorrelation times.
motivation: Traditional path integral Monte Carlo methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, especially for observables affected by permutation sampling.
method: The authors propose an exchange Monte Carlo algorithm that swaps configurations between multiple replicas at different temperatures to improve sampling efficiency.
result: The method reduces autocorrelation times and improves the accuracy of measurements in continuous-space PIMC simulations.
conclusion: Exchange Monte Carlo is an effective technique for enhancing sampling in continuous-space PIMC, enabling more efficient simulations of bosonic systems.

title: Further Testing The Validity Of Generalized Heterogeneous-elasticity Theory For Low-frequency Excitations In Structural Glasses

tldr: This paper tests the validity of generalized heterogeneous-elasticity theory for low-frequency excitations in structural glasses, focusing on nonuniversal scaling of the vibrational density of states.
motivation: Understanding low-frequency vibrational excitations in glasses is important for their mechanical and thermal properties, but the universality of scaling laws is debated.
method: The authors summarize their previous theory and provide further computational evidence by analyzing the nonphononic vibrational density of states and its scaling behavior in model glasses.
result: They find nonuniversal scaling of the nonphononic density of states, challenging the universality of the ω^4 law.
conclusion: The generalized heterogeneous-elasticity theory captures the observed nonuniversality, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Diffusion-driven Pattern Formation In An Opinion Dynamical Network Model
authors: Tim Mauch And Thilo Gross
abstract:

tldr: A network model of opinion formation with spatial structure, inspired by ecological metapopulation models, studies pattern formation in opinion dynamics.
motivation: To understand how spatial organization and community interactions preserve diversity in opinion dynamics, using a metapopulation-inspired network approach.
method: Develops a network model where nodes represent communities and edges represent interactions, analyzing diffusion-driven pattern formation via dynamical systems and bifurcation analysis.
result: Identifies conditions under which spatial patterns of opinions emerge, showing that community structure can stabilize diverse opinions.
conclusion: Spatial organization and network topology play a key role in maintaining opinion diversity, with implications for social systems and collective behavior.

title: Free-energy Model Of Ferroelectric Transition In P(VDF-TrFE) Copolymer
authors: Vadim V. Atrazhev, Dmitry V. Dmitriev, And Vadim I. Sultanov

We develop a physics-based analytical model for the ferroelectric-to-paraelectric phase transition in poly(vinylidene difluoride-co-trifluoroethylene) [P(VDF-TrFE)] copolymers. motivation: To understand the phase transition mechanism in ferroelectric polymers, which are important for applications like sensors and actuators.
method: Constructs a free-energy model based on the Landau-Devonshire theory, incorporating dipole interactions and thermal fluctuations.
result: The model reproduces the temperature dependence of polarization and dielectric constant, and predicts the transition temperature as a function of copolymer composition.
conclusion: The analytical model provides a quantitative description of the ferroelectric transition in P(VDF-TrFE) and can guide material design.

title: Externally Driven Condensates Show Translation-induced Polarization, Directed Coalescence, And Anomalous Diffusion In Viscoelastic Media
authors: Andriy Goychuk

tldr: This paper studies phase separation in externally driven condensates, focusing on polarization, coalescence, and anomalous diffusion in viscoelastic media.
motivation: Understanding how external driving forces control the organization and dynamics of phase-separated domains in soft matter and biological systems.
method: Theoretical modeling and numerical simulations of condensate dynamics under external fields in viscoelastic environments.
result: External driving induces translation-induced polarization, directed coalescence, and anomalous diffusion of condensates.
conclusion: External fields can be used to control condensate organization, with implications for nonequilibrium soft matter and biological phase separation.

title: Resetting-induced Instability In Queues Fed By A Search Process In An Interval
authors: José Giral-Barajas And Paul C. Bressloff
abstract:
Author(s): José Giral-Barajas and Paul C. Bressloff

tldr: This paper studies a queuing model where arrivals are governed by a search process with stochastic resetting, leading to instability.
motivation: To understand how resetting in search processes affects queue stability, relevant to resource management in random environments.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a queue fed by a search process with resetting, using generating functions and stability conditions.
result: Resetting can induce instability in the queue even when the underlying search process would otherwise be stable.
conclusion: Stochastic resetting can have counterintuitive effects on queue dynamics, with implications for natural and artificial systems.

title: Quantum Size Effect And Two-step Condensation Of Ideal Bose Atoms In An Optical Hard-wall Nanotube

method: Theoretical analysis using the grand canonical ensemble and solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a quasi-1D harmonic potential combined with a 2D box trap.
result: Predicts a two-step condensation process and quantum size effects due to the discrete energy levels in the confined geometry.
conclusion: The quasi-1D system exhibits unique condensation behavior that could be observed in ultracold atom experiments.

tldr: This paper studies oscillatory evolutionarily stable states and limit cycles in replicator dynamics from evolutionary game theory.

method: Uses replicator dynamics and mathematical analysis to characterize oscillatory solutions and their stability.
result: Identifies conditions under which limit cycles can be evolutionarily stable, generalizing the static ESS concept.
conclusion: Oscillatory states can be stable under replicator dynamics, providing a richer framework for evolutionary game theory.

title: Kinetic Decoupling In Electron-beam-driven Dusty Plasma: Microscopic Randomization Coexisting With Collective Flow Stability
authors: Adrian Scurtu, Dorina Ticoş, Nicoleta Udrea, Maria L. Mitu, Beatrice Paraschiv, And Cătălin M. Ticoş

motivation: To understand energy injection and dissipation in non-equilibrium systems, specifically the breakdown of synchrony between microscopic motion and collective flow.
method: Experimental observations of electron-beam-driven dusty plasma, analyzing microscopic and collective dynamics.
result: Discovery of a kinetic decoupling regime where microscopic randomization and collective flow stability coexist.
conclusion: The findings reveal a distinct regime in dusty plasma that challenges typical coupled evolution assumptions.

title: Reducibility Of Higher-order To Pairwise Interactions: Social Impact Models On Hypergraphs
authors: Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, And Federico Vázquez
abstract:
Author(s): Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, and Federico Vázquez

We show that a general class of node-update social impact models with higher-order interactions on hypergraphs can be exactly mapped to an equivalent model with pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023250] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.

motivation: To simplify the analysis of complex social systems with higher-order interactions by mapping them to well-understood pairwise models.
method: The authors prove an exact mapping from a class of node-update social impact models on hypergraphs to equivalent models with pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network, preserving microscopic transition probabilities.
result: The mapping is exact for the considered class of models, enabling the use of pairwise network tools to study higher-order social dynamics.
conclusion: Higher-order interactions in social impact models can be effectively reduced to pairwise interactions, simplifying theoretical and computational analysis.

title: Multiobjective Tweezers In Scattering Media

motivation: Controlling multiple objects in scattering media is challenging due to competing objectives and complex wave propagation.
method: The authors use wavefront shaping and optimization algorithms to simultaneously trap and manipulate multiple particles with acoustic waves in a scattering environment.
result: They achieve simultaneous trapping and independent control of multiple particles, demonstrating multiobjective tweezing in a complex medium.
conclusion: The approach extends wave-based manipulation to realistic scattering environments, enabling applications in biophysics and microfluidics.

title: Phenomenology Of Orbital Torque, Pumping, And Mixing Conductance In Metallic Bilayers

motivation: To understand the conversion between spin and orbital currents in magnetic bilayers, which is relevant for spintronic devices.
method: Develops a phenomenological model based on diffusion equations and boundary conditions to describe orbital torque and pumping.
result: Derives expressions for orbital torque, pumping, and mixing conductance, showing how orbital currents can generate torques.
conclusion: The model provides a framework for interpreting experiments on orbital torque and pumping in metallic bilayers.

title: From Knots To Crystals: Machine-learned Potentials For Self-assembling Topological Solitons In Liquid Crystals
authors: Arunkumar Bupathy, Darian Hall, Ivan I. Smalyukh, Gerardo Campos-Villalobos, Rodolfo Subert, And Marjolein Dijkstra

method: The authors develop machine-learned interaction potentials from molecular simulations and use them to simulate the self-assembly of heliknoton solitons into crystalline structures.
result: They demonstrate that heliknotons can form stable crystals with tunable properties, and the machine-learned potentials accurately capture their interactions.
conclusion: Machine-learned potentials enable efficient study of topological soliton assemblies, opening avenues for designing novel liquid crystal materials.

title: Are Neural Networks Collision Resistant?
authors: Marco Benedetti, Andrej Bogdanov, Enrico M. Malatesta, Marc Mézard, Gianmarco Perrupato, Alon Rosen, Nikolaj I. Schwartzbach, And Riccardo Zecchina

method: The authors analyze the computational complexity of finding collisions in a simple one-layer neural network, likely using techniques from computational complexity theory and statistical physics.
result: Efficient algorithms fail to find collisions, suggesting that such neural networks may be collision resistant.
conclusion: The findings are relevant for defining new cryptographic protocols based on machine-learning models.

authors: Hongwei Zhang, Chunsheng Wang, Ran Wang, Senyang Pan, Hengning Wang, Jiaqiang Cai, Yonglai Liu, Zhe Qu, Xiangde Zhu, Wei Ning, Chuanying Xi, Jinglei Zhang, Ning Hao, Guolin Zheng, And Mingliang Tian

authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature, characterized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but many are only stable at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature platform for studying such phenomena.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to map the electronic band structure, revealing flat bands that persist at room temperature.
result: Intrinsic orbital-selective flat bands are observed that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.
conclusion: These materials offer a promising system for exploring flat-band physics and potentially correlated phases at accessible temperatures.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve performance.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to detect anisotropy and its response to heat treatment.
result: They find hidden anisotropy in silica films that resists standard heat treatment, informing coating design and postprocessing strategies.
conclusion: The discovery guides the development of coatings with reduced thermal noise for gravitational-wave detectors.

tldr: This paper reports the observation of intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a bulk insulator using multimodal optical characterization.

authors: Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, And Jonathan Pelliciari

motivation: To understand the nature of photoinduced hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems, which may have implications for novel electronic phases.
method: Ultrafast photoexcitation combined with resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to probe excitations in the equilibrium and hidden phases of Pr0.67Ca0.33MnO3.

conclusion: Photoexcitation can stabilize hidden phases with distinct lattice and electronic excitations, offering a route to control material properties.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order interactions, using evolutionary game theory and epidemic modeling.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social reinforcement influences vaccination uptake and epidemic outcomes.
method: A two-layer multiplex model with an SIR epidemic on a square lattice and a hypergraph for triadic social interactions, where individuals update vaccination strategies via imitation with reinforcement modulation.
result: Higher-order structure creates vaccinated clusters; small reinforcement maximizes coverage and suppresses outbreaks, while too strong or zero reinforcement reduces uptake.
conclusion: The non-monotonic effect of reinforcement suggests that moderate local inhibition balances adaptability and protection.

title: Emergent Hydrodynamics Of Chiral Active Fluids: Vortices, Bubbles And Odd Diffusion
authors: Umberto Marini Bettolo Marconi, Alessandro Petrini, Raphael Maire And Lorenzo Caprini
abstract: Starting from a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation, we obtain a hydrodynamic description in terms of density and momentum fields for chiral active particles interacting via standard repulsive and nonlocal odd forces. These odd interactions are reciprocal but non-conservative: they are non-potential forces, as they act perpendicular to the vector joining any pair of particles. As a result, the torques that two particles exert on one another are non-reciprocal. The ensuing macroscopic continuum description consists of a continuity equation for the density and a generalized compressible Navier–Stokes equation for the fluid velocity. The latter includes a chirality-induced torque density term and an odd viscosity contribution. Our theory predicts the emergence of odd diffusivity, edge currents, and is consistent with an inhomogeneous phase—characterized by bubble-like structures—recently observed in simulations. Specifically, the theory exhibits a linear instability arising from the interplay between odd viscosity and torque density, and admits steady-state inhomogeneous solutions featuring bubbles and vortices, in qualitative agreement with numerical simulations. Our findings can be tested experimentally in systems of granular spinners or rotating microorganisms suspended in a fluid.
tldr: Derives hydrodynamic equations for chiral active fluids with odd interactions, predicting odd diffusivity and bubble-vortex phases.
motivation: To understand collective behavior in chiral active matter systems such as granular spinners or rotating microorganisms.
method: Coarse-graining a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation with repulsive and odd forces to obtain continuum density and momentum equations.
result: The theory yields odd viscosity, odd diffusivity, edge currents, and a linear instability leading to inhomogeneous bubble-like structures and vortices.
conclusion: The hydrodynamic description captures emergent phenomena in chiral active fluids and can be tested experimentally.

title: Passive All-optical Synchronization For Polarization-maintaining Ultrafast Fiber Lasers
authors: Kun Huang, Jing Zeng, Jiwei Gan, Qiang Hao, Ming Yan, Heping Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have proposed and implemented for the first time to our best knowledge a passive and all-optical pulse synchronization for polarization-maintaining ultrafast fiber lasers. Specifically, the synchronization system was comprised of two independent Yb-doped and Er-doped mode-locked fiber lasers in a master-slave configuration. Master pulses were injected into the slave laser cavity consisting of a nonlinear amplifying loop mirror, which provided an effective fast intensity modulator due to the periodic introduction of nonreciprocal phase difference. As a result, robust and tight timing synchronization was achieved with a cavity mismatch tolerance of 800 [MATH]m and a relative timing jitter of 26 fs within 1-MHz bandwidth. In combination with all-polarization-maintaining structure of fiber lasers, long-term stable operation was demonstrated over 12 hours without the need of temperature stabilization and vibration isolation. The implemented synchronous laser system could find immediate applications such as pump-probe microscopy, two-color spectroscopy and nonlinear frequency mixing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates passive all-optical synchronization of two polarization-maintaining ultrafast fiber lasers using a master-slave configuration with a nonlinear amplifying loop mirror.
motivation: To achieve robust, low-jitter synchronization of ultrafast lasers without active electronics, enabling applications like pump-probe microscopy and two-color spectroscopy.
method: Two independent Yb-doped and Er-doped mode-locked fiber lasers are synchronized by injecting master pulses into the slave laser cavity, which contains a nonlinear amplifying loop mirror that acts as a fast intensity modulator via nonreciprocal phase difference.
result: The system achieves a cavity mismatch tolerance of 800 μm and a relative timing jitter of 26 fs within 1-MHz bandwidth, with stable operation over 12 hours without temperature stabilization or vibration isolation.
conclusion: The passive all-optical synchronization method is effective and robust, suitable for practical applications requiring stable dual-color ultrafast laser sources.

title: Ultralow Shot Noise Limited Giant Passive Resonant Gyroscope For Earth Rotation Measurement
authors: Yuhong Zhong, Yangsheng Cai, Zhanhao Liu, Lei Zheng, Yunhe Wang, Xiaojun Huang, Zhiyuan Wang, Kui Liu, Liangcheng Tu, Jun Luo, Zehuang Lu, Jie Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical gyroscopes directly measure the Earth's rotation and are promising instruments for real-time geophysical observations and Earth orientation parameter (EOP) determination requiring both high precision and high temporal resolution. Large-scale ring laser gyroscopes (RLGs) currently reach rotational resolutions around [MATH], but their quantum noise limits make it challenging to meet the requirements of future high-temporal-resolution EOP measurements. Passive resonant gyroscopes (PRGs), on the other hand, offer a potentially lower photon shot noise limit and more flexible power scaling, even if their demonstrated rotational resolutions are still about two orders of magnitude below those of leading RLGs. Here we demonstrate a [MATH] giant passive resonant gyroscope HUST-2, and develop with an extremely low shot noise level. We experimentally obtain a shot noise limited of [MATH] at [MATH] incident optical power, following the characteristic [MATH] scaling. Through systematic suppression of dominant technical noise sources, HUST-2 further achieves a measured rotational resolution of [MATH], bringing PRGs into the performance regime of leading large-scale RLGs for the first time. The gap between the present demonstrated rotational resolution and the shot noise limit indicates nearly two orders of magnitude further improvement potential. Reaching this limit would enable high-precision length-of-day (LOD) measurements with [MATH]-[MATH] temporal resolution and lays the foundation for future large-scale gyroscope networks dedicated to real-time EOP determination.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a giant passive resonant gyroscope for Earth rotation measurement, achieving ultralow shot noise and high rotational resolution.
motivation: To improve the precision and temporal resolution of Earth rotation measurements for geophysical observations and Earth orientation parameter determination.
method: A 3-meter giant passive resonant gyroscope (HUST-2) is built, and technical noise sources are systematically suppressed to approach the shot noise limit.
result: The gyroscope achieves a rotational resolution of 1.2×10⁻⁹ rad/s, matching leading ring laser gyroscopes, with a shot noise limit of 4.5×10⁻¹¹ rad/s at 1 W optical power.
conclusion: Passive resonant gyroscopes can rival ring laser gyroscopes in performance and offer further improvement potential for high-temporal-resolution Earth rotation measurements.

title: Flash: Ultrafast Beam Quality Characterization Via Spatial-to-temporal Mapping
authors: J. Qiu, Y. Xiong, X. Hua, H. Wu, M. Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and real-time monitoring of spatial beam quality has emerged as the absolute prerequisite for intelligent optical field regulation and advanced laser applications. However, modern high-power and multimode optical systems exhibit highly complex, nonlinear, and transient behaviors. In these systems, the spatial beam profile undergoes dramatic reorganizations within extremely short timeframes. Phenomena such as spatio-temporal mode-locking, transient beam self-cleaning, and plasma-induced aberrations demand nanosecond-level dynamic characterization. Yet, capturing these ultrafast dynamics is fundamentally bottlenecked by the kilohertz frame rates of conventional two-dimensional image sensors. To break this dimensional and temporal barrier, we propose an ultrafast non-imaging beam quality monitoring technique, termed Fiber-based Laser Assessment via Spatial-to-temporal High-speed-mapping (FLASH). By utilizing a multimode fiber to encode spatial beam variations into high-dimensional speckle fingerprints and a multicore fiber delay line array to serialize these features, we transform two-dimensional spatial information into high-speed one-dimensional temporal pulse sequences. Empowered by a deep learning model to decipher the serialized signals, the FLASH system achieves an unprecedented 100 MHz measurement rate with a minimal mean relative error of 0.32%. Realizing a five-order-of-magnitude speed improvement over standard camera-based methods, this spatial-to-temporal mapping paradigm provides a transformative spatial oscilloscope. It unlocks new possibilities for real-time intelligent adaptive control and the exploration of complex multimode nonlinear physics.
tldr: A technique using multimode fiber and deep learning to characterize laser beam quality at 100 MHz, far exceeding camera-based methods.
motivation: High-power multimode lasers exhibit ultrafast spatial beam dynamics that conventional cameras cannot capture due to kilohertz frame rates.
method: Spatial beam variations are encoded into speckle patterns via a multimode fiber, serialized by a multicore fiber delay line, and decoded by a deep learning model.
result: Achieves 100 MHz measurement rate with 0.32% mean relative error, a five-order-of-magnitude speed improvement over standard cameras.
conclusion: This spatial-to-temporal mapping paradigm enables real-time adaptive control and study of complex multimode nonlinear physics.

title: Smooth Hard-Thresholding For Singular Values With Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate
authors: Guanzhong Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-rank matrix denoising is a central primitive in patch-based image restoration and many other inverse problems. Classical SVD-based image denoising methods often choose a truncation rank by matching residual singular-value energy with an estimated noise energy, but this rule is not a finite-sample risk principle because a fitted low-rank approximation inevitably absorbs part of the noise. This paper develops a mathematically rigorous alternative based on Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE). Since singular value hard thresholding is discontinuous and does not satisfy the hypotheses of Stein's lemma, we introduce a logistic smooth hard-threshold spectral estimator. We prove that the smooth shrinker satisfies the regularity conditions required by a spectral-estimator version of Stein's lemma, and therefore admits an exactly unbiased fixed-threshold risk estimate under Gaussian noise. For a fixed observed matrix and a finite set of candidate thresholds separated from the observed singular values, the ordering of the fixed-threshold smooth SURE objective eventually agrees with a simple limiting score. The limiting score has the same algebraic form as the biased hard-threshold SURE formula, but here it is used only as a computational device for ranking finite candidates. Selecting the minimizing threshold is a data-adaptive tuning step; the selected SURE value should not be interpreted as an unbiased risk estimate of the finally selected estimator.
tldr: This paper develops a smooth hard-thresholding estimator for singular values in low-rank matrix denoising, using Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE) for threshold selection.
motivation: Classical SVD-based denoising methods lack a finite-sample risk principle because the fitted low-rank approximation absorbs noise. The authors aim to provide a mathematically rigorous alternative.
method: They introduce a logistic smooth hard-threshold spectral estimator that satisfies Stein's lemma regularity conditions, enabling an unbiased risk estimate for fixed thresholds. They also derive a limiting score for ranking candidate thresholds.
result: The smooth SURE objective eventually agrees with a simple limiting score for finite candidate thresholds, and the minimizing threshold can be selected data-adaptively.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a principled approach to threshold selection in low-rank matrix denoising, though the selected SURE value is not an unbiased estimate of the final estimator's risk.

title: Spectral And Essential Spectral Analysis Of Finite-Rank Perturbations Of Unbounded Diagonal Operators On Non-Archimedean Hilbert Spaces
authors: Teylama Miabey
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the spectral properties of a class of unbounded linear operators on a non-Archimedean Hilbert space [MATH]. More precisely, we consider operators of the form \[ T=D+F,\qquad F=\sum_{j=1}^{m} u_j\otimes v_j, \] where [MATH] is an unbounded diagonal operator and [MATH] is a finite-rank perturbation. This work extends the spectral analysis of Diagana and McNeal for rank-one perturbations of diagonal operators to the case of arbitrary finite-rank perturbations. The main objective is to describe the spectrum, point spectrum, and essential spectrum of such operators in terms of the diagonal sequence associated with [MATH] and the Fredholm properties of [MATH]. The theory of Fredholm operators plays a central role, particularly in the computation of the essential spectrum and in the study of stability under finite-rank perturbations.
tldr: This paper studies spectral properties of finite-rank perturbations of unbounded diagonal operators on non-Archimedean Hilbert spaces, extending prior work to arbitrary finite-rank perturbations.
motivation: To generalize spectral analysis of rank-one perturbations to finite-rank perturbations in non-Archimedean Hilbert spaces, which is a purely mathematical topic.
method: Uses Fredholm operator theory to describe the spectrum, point spectrum, and essential spectrum in terms of the diagonal sequence and Fredholm properties.
result: Provides a description of the spectrum and essential spectrum for such operators, showing stability under finite-rank perturbations.
conclusion: The work extends known results to a more general setting, but remains within abstract functional analysis without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Environment-Division Multiple Access: An Enabler For AI-Native Multiple Access
authors: Zhiguo Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, a new type of multiple access, termed Environment-Division Multiple Access (EDMA), is introduced and its interaction with AI-native communication networks is illustrated. In particular, the key properties of EDMA, such as utilizing the features of wireless propagation environments, integrating advanced flexible antennas, and proactively reconfiguring propagation environments, are described. The article also illustrates two types of applications of AI tools to multiple access, namely AI-assisted EDMA and AI-native EDMA. Finally, open problems and important directions for future research in AI-assisted EDMA are discussed.
tldr: This paper introduces Environment-Division Multiple Access (EDMA), a new multiple access technique for AI-native communication networks.
motivation: To address the need for efficient multiple access in future AI-native wireless networks by leveraging environmental features and reconfigurable propagation environments.
method: The paper describes the concept of EDMA, its key properties (utilizing wireless propagation environments, integrating advanced antennas, proactively reconfiguring environments), and discusses AI-assisted and AI-native EDMA approaches.
result: EDMA is proposed as a new multiple access paradigm that can be enhanced by AI tools, with open problems identified for future research.
conclusion: EDMA offers a promising direction for AI-native multiple access, but the paper is a conceptual overview without technical depth or experimental validation.

title: A Unified DeepONet Framework For Logarithmically Stable Infinite-Dimensional Inverse Problems
authors: Wen-Jie Wu, Tiexiang Li, Wen-Wei Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a unified DeepONet framework for logarithmically stable infinite-dimensional inverse problems, with inverse acoustic scattering as a model application. The framework is formulated at the operator level by separating the learned inverse map into measurement encoding, finite-dimensional neural approximation, and functional reconstruction components. For inverse maps satisfying a logarithmic stability estimate, we establish quantitative a priori error bounds giving separate estimates for the encoder error, the neural approximation error, and the reconstruction error, thereby characterizing the dependence on the encoder dimension, the network size, and the reconstruction dimension. For comparison, we also record the corresponding Lipschitz-stable estimate arising from the same error decomposition. The abstract theory is then specialized to the recovery of a medium contrast from fixed-frequency far-field measurements. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions illustrate stable reconstructions under measurement noise.
tldr: A unified DeepONet framework for logarithmically stable infinite-dimensional inverse problems, applied to inverse acoustic scattering.
motivation: Inverse problems often suffer from instability; the authors aim to develop a neural network framework that leverages logarithmic stability for robust reconstruction.
method: They propose a DeepONet-based architecture that separates the inverse map into measurement encoding, finite-dimensional neural approximation, and functional reconstruction, with theoretical error bounds.
result: Quantitative a priori error bounds are established, and numerical experiments in 2D and 3D demonstrate stable reconstructions under noise.
conclusion: The framework provides a principled approach to solving logarithmically stable inverse problems with neural networks, with potential extensions to other applications.

title: Numerical Approximation Of The Stochastic Cahn--Hilliard Equation With Singular Potential
authors: Stefan Metzger \v{l}ubom\'ir Ba\v{n}as
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss the numerical approximation of the stochastic Cahn--Hilliard equation with a singular double-obstacle potential and multiplicative conservative noise. We propose a regularised fully discrete finite element approximation scheme for the problem and show that it satisfies stability estimates which are uniform with respect to the discretization parameters. We show convergence of the approximation for vanishing discretization parameters towards a regularised version of the singular stochastic Cahn--Hilliard equation by monotonicity arguments. Hence, thanks to a uniform [MATH]-estimate for the regularised problem we show that the regularised solution converges towards the pathwise unique probabilistically strong solution of the original singular stochastic Cahn--Hilliard equation. We conclude by presenting numerical simulations where we compare the regularised numerical approximation to its unregularised counterpart and illustrate the effect of the conservative noise.
tldr: This paper develops a numerical approximation scheme for the stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation with a singular potential and multiplicative noise.
motivation: The stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation models phase separation under thermal fluctuations, but its singular potential poses numerical challenges.
method: A regularized finite element scheme is proposed, with stability and convergence proofs via monotonicity and uniform estimates.
result: The regularized approximation converges to the unique strong solution of the original singular equation as discretization parameters vanish.
conclusion: The scheme is effective for simulating the stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation with singular potentials, as demonstrated by numerical experiments.

title: Enhancing Malware Detection With Generative Ai: Using Variational Autoencoders To Boost Machine Learning Classifiers' Performance
authors: Jeremy Straub Mohammad Alharbi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.06501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The advancement of malware poses obstacles for cybersecurity, necessitating the development of advanced detection techniques. This paper proposes an approach to enhance malware detection through the use of a generative artificial intelligence model. Specifically, variational autoencoders (VAEs) are used with the random forest, XGBoost and sequential model machine learning classifiers. Generated synthetic malware samples are used to address the critical issue of data scarcity for new or less common malware types. This approach can be used to augment datasets to improve classifier robustness. The proposed methodology uses VAEs to create high-quality diverse synthetic datasets that closely mimic real-world malware data. The effectiveness of these augmented datasets is evaluated by comparing the performance of the machine learning classifiers when they are trained with the original data and when they are trained with the synthetic data-augmented datasets. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in the accuracy, precision, recall and F1-scores of the classifiers, when they are trained using the augmented datasets. The enhanced performance for detecting various malware classes shows the potential of this approach to facilitate adaptation to evolving malware threats effectively. This work demonstrates the utility of generative AI for cybersecurity. It also provides a foundation for future research aimed at developing more resilient and adaptive malware detection systems.
tldr: This paper uses variational autoencoders to generate synthetic malware samples for augmenting training data, improving machine learning classifiers for malware detection.
motivation: Malware detection faces data scarcity for new or rare malware types, limiting classifier robustness.
method: Variational autoencoders generate synthetic malware samples; these augment original datasets to train random forest, XGBoost, and sequential models.
result: Augmented datasets improve accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores across classifiers for various malware classes.
conclusion: Generative AI can enhance malware detection by addressing data imbalance and improving classifier adaptability to evolving threats.

title: Evidence Markets
authors: Safwan Hossain, Gabriel Andrade, Chengqi Zang, Yiling Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.07434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern prediction markets face two limitations that restrict their applicability in a range of settings:~(i)~they reveal what the crowd believes but not the evidence or reasoning behind those beliefs, and~(ii)~they require an event with an external ground truth that resolves at a known future date. We address these twin challenges by introducing evidence markets, a generalization of prediction markets that incentivizes the submission of evidence alongside beliefs and can be endogenously resolved using the crowd-sourced evidence if external resolution is not possible. At its core, the market uses a logarithmic market scoring rule whose liquidity parameter changes dynamically with the accumulated evidence quality. We prove that platform loss is bounded, evidence is rewarded proportional to the current market uncertainty, and can be equivalently implemented through an automated market maker. In the case where the marker resolves endogenously based on submitted evidence, we characterize how withholding evidence shifts a trader's belief about resolution and use it to prove truthful belief and evidence reporting is a always an [MATH]-dominant strategy incentive compatible (DSIC) strategy. To address operational considerations, we propose evidence verification via an LLM-as-a-Judge framework with staking and give an asynchronous execution algorithm that is not bottle-necked by verification. Throughout the work, we use LLM evaluations -- determining which model is best for a given task -- as a salient and representative running example for our proposed market.
tldr: Introduces evidence markets, a generalization of prediction markets that incentivizes submission of evidence and can resolve endogenously using crowd-sourced evidence.
motivation: Modern prediction markets reveal beliefs but not evidence, and require external ground truth; evidence markets address these limitations.
method: Uses a logarithmic market scoring rule with dynamic liquidity parameter based on accumulated evidence quality; proposes LLM-as-a-Judge for evidence verification.
result: Proves bounded platform loss, evidence reward proportional to uncertainty, and truthful reporting as a DSIC strategy under endogenous resolution.
conclusion: Evidence markets can elicit both beliefs and evidence, with applications in LLM evaluation and other settings lacking external ground truth.

tldr: This paper reports a super-resolution imaging technique using photoblinking in upconversion nanoparticles, achieving 30 nm resolution in biological cells.

title: Is Ball Lightning A Relativistic Soliton?
authors: Sergei Bulanov

Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism can improve reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: A coherent model emerges where tiny surface defects, electric stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdown.
conclusion: Insights from this model can help design more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of the physics and chemistry of transplutonium elements under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and behavior.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear power and waste management, and their 5f electrons exhibit unique localized/itinerant behavior under pressure.
method: The paper reviews experimental and theoretical studies of metals, alloys, compounds, and coordination complexes under high pressure.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of pressure-induced changes in electronic structure, bonding, and phase transitions in transplutonium materials.
conclusion: High-pressure studies reveal complex behavior in transplutonium elements, but the field remains challenging due to radioactivity and electron correlation effects.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to nuclear astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper surveys detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and discusses simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It highlights the potential for multimessenger observations to improve understanding of dense matter in neutron stars.
conclusion: Multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves will become increasingly important with next-generation detectors.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is not accessible in terrestrial experiments.
method: Review of recent gravitational-wave detections from binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are presented, showing consistency with some nuclear models but leaving uncertainties at higher densities.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state, but current data already provide important insights into dense matter.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Nobel lecture by John Hopfield reflecting on his career and the nature of physics as a point of view.
motivation: To share personal insights and perspectives on physics research, particularly neural networks and associative memory.
method: Narrative and reflective lecture, not a technical research paper.
result: No new scientific results; discusses the evolution of ideas in physics and computation.
conclusion: Physics is a way of thinking that can lead to discoveries across disciplines.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is the Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, a foundational concept in machine learning and neural networks.
motivation: To present the development and significance of Boltzmann machines, which are stochastic neural networks that learn probability distributions.
method: The lecture describes the architecture, training algorithm (contrastive divergence), and theoretical underpinnings of Boltzmann machines.
result: Boltzmann machines can learn complex distributions and have been influential in deep learning, but the lecture does not present new research results.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines remain a key concept in machine learning, but the paper is a retrospective lecture, not a research contribution.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights capabilities and limitations of each technique and cases where combining them yields more comprehensive disorder characterization.
conclusion: Real-space microscopy techniques, especially when combined, provide valuable atomic-scale disorder information for semiconductor materials.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonance phenomena.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions at stellar energies is crucial for astrophysics but experimentally challenging due to low rates.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects.
result: Provides an overview of the state-of-the-art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory.
conclusion: New experimental and theoretical methods are needed to study these reactions on Earth.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data.
motivation: Accurate and self-consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, requiring periodic updates as new measurements become available.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a global dataset of measurements and theoretical calculations, incorporating correlations and uncertainties to produce recommended values.
result: The 2022 set of recommended values for constants such as the Planck constant, elementary charge, and Boltzmann constant, along with their uncertainties, is provided.
conclusion: The CODATA recommended values serve as the authoritative reference for fundamental constants, supporting precision measurements and theoretical work across physics and chemistry.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. A complete understanding of the creases and sharp cusps that commonly accompany buckling requires nonlinear elasticity theory. This review presents a modern treatment of the Biot instability, integrating many standard techniques of nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015004] Published Mon Feb 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of buckling instabilities in growing soft matter using nonlinear elasticity theory.
motivation: Understanding creases and cusps in soft materials is important for morphogenesis and materials science.
method: The review integrates bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and nonlinear elasticity to analyze the Biot instability.
result: Provides a modern treatment of buckling patterns in growing soft matter.
conclusion: Nonlinear elasticity is essential to fully describe the observed instabilities.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools for constructing and using Wannier functions in electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys the ecosystem of software packages (e.g., Wannier90) and their applications, describing the underlying theory and interoperability.
result: It catalogs the capabilities of the ecosystem, including applications to topological invariants, Berry phases, and accurate integrations.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling a wide range of materials simulations.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
authors: I. H. Hutchinson
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior.
